About this work

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem — "A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian" — is Trithemius's reply to eight questions the Emperor set him (by his own account at the castle of Boppard): on faith and reason, on the faith necessary for salvation, on the miracles worked by unbelievers, on witches and malefic magic, and on related theological and natural-philosophical points. Composed in 1508 and printed in 1515, it is his principal statement on witchcraft and the work through which his demonology passed into early-modern learned culture. The eight questions are enumerated at the head of the book and answered in turn.

This is the 1550 Frankfurt edition (BSB scan) — a later reprint of the text first printed at Oppenheim in 1515. It is one of four witnesses of the Octo Quaestionum in this corpus: the 1515 Oppenheim first edition (prdl-24382), the 1534 Cologne edition (prdl-32286), the 1601 Mainz edition (prdl-70286), and this 1550 Frankfurt reprint. BOOK OF EIGHT QUESTIONS TO EMPEROR MAXIMILIAN, BY JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SAINT JAMES at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim.

On faith and understanding. On the faith necessary for salvation. On the miracles of unbelievers. On sacred Scripture. On the reprobate and evildoers. On the power of witches. On divine permission. On the providence of God. 1550.

TO THE MOST SERENE AND UNCONQUERED LORD OF THE WORLD, EMPEROR MAXIMILIAN, THE BOOK OF EIGHT QUESTIONS BY JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF PEAPOLIS. IN THE NAME OF CHRIST IT BEGINS.

I have obeyed your commands, most unconquered Emperor Maximilian, and have resolved, with what brevity I could, those eight questions which you proposed to me some time ago when I was summoned to your highness at the castle of Boppard; I have set them down in this little book. You wished, moreover, if I remember correctly, that, so far as could be done in their solution, I should follow the path of nature, on account of those who grant less to belief. Yet this did not seem possible to me in all respects, because the subject matter of the questions in many places rested on theological rather than natural principles.

For although the Christian religion, among all the sects of mortals, is held to be nearer, more conformable, and closer to the laws of nature, nevertheless the principal articles of our faith are not all provable according to the common path of nature. We necessarily believe that this was done so that faith might have its place, and firm belief not lack its own merit. Therefore, entering at your command upon a middle way of disputation, so far as my strength allowed, I have made use partly of nature and partly also of the testimony of the divine Scriptures. For indeed those things which it is fitting for us to believe must not rashly be examined by human arguments, since, as Saint Gregory says, faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof. Therefore, with fear of God and reverence for our undefiled Christian religion, I have undertaken to answer the proposed questions in such a way that I depart from the definitions of the Roman Church neither in jest nor in earnest. Hence whatever I have ever written, or shall write, I wish the whole of it to be subject to its determination and judgment.

ON FAITH AND UNDERSTANDING. THE FIRST QUESTION.

Question First

The first question of your most serene majesty was this: why did almighty God wish to be believed by mortals rather than known and understood, namely in that mode of knowledge and understanding by which he is known and understood by the holy angels?

I remember that I answered this question of your most sacred majesty, when it was put before me in person, as follows. Almighty God, who is without beginning, pure intellect, everlasting and unchangeable, existing above every position knowable to us, far more perfect than infinite perfections, by his most wise will created from nothing two intellects from the beginning, namely the angelic and the human. The angelic intellect, at the beginning of its creation, was made in the actuality of all knowable things, and knew all things. The human intellect, however, at first indeed consists in the potentiality of all things, but was ignorant of all things. Yet in the end, through very many continuous actions upward, it will become like the angelic, knowing both God and all things that pertain to the knowledge of the promised cognition and understanding. The two intellects, the angelic and the human, differ as any two opposites do: namely as actuality and potentiality, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, possession and privation, beginning and end, immobile and mobile, substance and accident, truth and likeness, nature and art, health and sickness, whole and part. For the angelic intellect is like actuality, light, knowledge, possession, beginning, immobile, immediate, simple substance, truth, nature, and the whole. The human intellect, however, is like potentiality, darkness, ignorance, privation, end, mobile, mediated, composite, accident, likeness, art, and part. Hence whatever belongs to the angelic intellect from the beginning, these same things are present in the human intellect at the end, after it has laid aside the burden of the flesh; for just as beginning and nature perfect the angelic intellect, so the end and art, after many exercises, at last raise the human intellect upward. Therefore between these two intellects there is great inequality from the beginning; yet in the end they are at last made equal, when the human intellect will be as great by art as the angelic intellect came before it by nature. Hence it is clear that the angelic intellect, as soon as it was created— it was created, from the beginning, without any action or motion of its own, immovably, substantially, and by nature, it knew all things that it can understand, and came forth created in an instant, full and perfect in the knowledge of all things. But because the human intellect was created in ignorance and privation of all things, and for its own exercise was assigned for a time to the body, it must arrive at knowledge of God and of all things by continual action, motion, and art. The end will at last make it equal to the angelic intellect, changing its potency into act; and, bringing it out from mere potency and possibility into essence, it will make it full from empty, perfect from imperfect, possessing from deprived, luminous from dark, diurnal from nocturnal, solar from lunar, and heavenly from earthly. This cannot happen while the mind is bound together with the body, as the holy God-loving Paul says: “As long as we are in the flesh, we are pilgrims away from the Lord.” To know God belongs to a pure, simple, and perfect intellect; but the human intellect, as long as it remains in the body, is impure, mixed, unstable, and imperfect, and for this reason, without faith, ignorant of all knowledge of God and of heavenly things. Yet the object of both intellects, namely the human and the angelic, is the same the same object, namely that highest immutable good, God, the one principle of all things, to which they return by a natural affection for knowledge. But if the angelic intellect is compared with the human, it is as nature is to art, and as intellect simply so called is to reason: intellect touches the principles of the disciplines, whereas reason runs through principles to conclusions. Hence it is clear that the angelic intellect immovably apprehends its proper object; but the human intellect, after many exercises of itself, as has been said, at last in time runs toward that object through the angelic medium and prepares an ascent for itself. The human intellect is separated, by the angelic as medium, from the cognitive perfection of its natural object, and therefore necessarily becomes mobile, returning through that medium to its own principle. For every motion from one extreme to another takes place through a middle; but where there is no middle, the extremes are already immediate and near, and therefore immovable. The human intellect, however, placed as it were in a dark prison so long as it is held in the body, is moved to understanding by sense and reason, although very confusedly and imperfectly, and therefore admits a middle between itself and God, which we have called angelic, while it bears the body, the obstacle to its destined perfection, as a certain lover of wisdom said: “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks many things.” Therefore it was wholly necessary for us to believe God rather than to know or understand him, because it is utterly impossible for us to comprehend that super-divine and uncircumscribable majesty, we who understand nothing without the service of the senses and the discourse of reason. But God, existing far above every position, remains subject neither to the senses of mortals nor to reason, just as he is read to have said to Moses: “A man shall not see me and live.” Hence also the divine evangelist John says: “No one has ever seen God.” Nor is this surprising. For since God is the first and eternal intellect, most pure, most simple, most perfect, immovable, creator, incomprehensible, highest, immeasurable far above every position, and uncircumscribable, he could not be comprehended by the human intellect, which is impure, subject to composition, imperfect, mobile, created, comprehensible, lowest, and constituted under the measure of position.

To that question, however, which seemed to arise from the first, namely whether God, since he is omnipotent, could have made himself knowable to the human intellect as to the angelic intellect, I say that no one of sound mind has ever denied that God can do all things. Yet we say that God cannot do those things which involve contradiction, because they are contrary to the order of the wisdom of him who immutably disposes all things, just as destruction is undoubtedly contrary to the construction of the whole at the same time, and, if I may say so, wholly opposed to it. For it was neither fitting nor in any way possible that God should be comprehended by the human intellect, since if mortal man, by the guidance of nature, comprehended the immortal God, he would certainly now seem to have to be called not man nor mortal, but an angel, and either man would be made comparable to God or God to man. For so long as the angelic intellect stands between, the human intellect cannot understand God. It stands between until the death of the flesh; when the mind, having obtained natural freedom, will become altogether equal to an angel. I think you now see clearly, emperor, that it was neither fitting nor possible that the human intellect should comprehend the divine; that the created should comprehend the creator, the temporal the eternal, the changeable the unchangeable, the weak the omnipotent, since, as a certain philosopher says, there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite. It is therefore necessary for mortals to believe in the immortal God, whom we can comprehend by no evident reasoning. Although the order of the whole universe declares its provident author in all things, and we understand that nothing except him has been brought into being without a beginning, nevertheless the human mind cannot grasp what God is and how he is God; for since he is far above all things that we can understand concerning him, or that any mortal can understand, he is far beyond and above every position, as holy Dionysius says. For he is neither soul, nor sense, nor does he have imagination or opinion, or reason, or understanding; nor is he reason, nor understanding; nor is he spoken, nor understood. Nor is he number, nor multitude, nor order, nor greatness, nor smallness, nor equality, nor likeness, nor unlikeness; nor does he stand, nor is he moved; nor does he produce rest; nor does he have power, nor is he power; nor is he light; nor does he live; nor is he life; nor is he substance, nor age, nor time; nor is there spiritual contact with him; nor is he form, nor truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom, nor one, nor unity, nor deity or goodness; nor is he spirit, so far as we ourselves can know. Nor is there denomination of son or father, nor anything else among those things which are known to us or to anyone else in the world. Nor is he anything of those things which are not, nor of those things which are. Nor do the things that are know him as he himself is. There is no speech of him, nor name, nor knowledge; nor is he darkness, nor light, nor error, nor truth; nor is there any position at all concerning him, nor any removal. For he is above every position, the perfect and singular cause of all things. And above every removal is his excellence, namely of him who is simply absolved from all things and is above all things. Therefore, Dionysius says, we say that, since the cause of all things is above all things, he is neither without substance nor without life, nor does he lack reason or mind, nor is he body, nor figure. nor species, nor does he have quality or quantity or mass. He is not in a place, nor is he seen, nor does he have sensible touch, nor does he sense, nor is he sensible, nor is he liable to rashness or disturbance, as though agitated by carnal passions. Nor is he weak, subject to sensible accidents; nor is he in need of light; nor does he admit change or corruption, or division, or flux; nor is he, or does he have, anything else belonging to sensible things. Hence, since he excels far above every position, he could not be comprehended by the creature set beneath him, which necessarily uses the senses for understanding, as the true Peripatetic said: there is nothing in our intellect unless it has first been in sense. Therefore God, who is not subject to the senses of mortals, far exceeds the human intellect: according to affirmative position he truly is entirely in all things; and according to negative removal, the nearer one approaches, he is none of all the things that are subject to the cognition of mortals. Indeed, since he is above all things, he can be none of those things that are subject to him. Therefore Empedocles beautifully gave the comparison, saying: God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. Let the human intellect now raise itself as much as it can, and let the person who strives to comprehend God comprehend, if he understands rightly, at once the center of this imagined sphere and its circumference, which terminates nowhere. But if he is not able properly to understand this proposition of the comparison, why does he contend to investigate the essence of God, which exists above every position? May it not weary you, most unconquered Caesar, to hear another comparison concerning God from Nicholas of Cusa, once priest and cardinal of the Roman Church, my fellow Mosellan, a man most learned in those times, who says: God is a straight line of infinite length which makes a circle. Let us now consider, then. If it is a straight line, how does it make a circle? But if it makes a circle, how is it straight? For a circle and a straight line are naturally opposed. Nevertheless a line of infinite length, since it has neither beginning nor end, necessarily makes a circle, although it is proposed to be imagined not as curved but as straight. Therefore, since God is infinite, greatest without quantity, best without quality, all things in all things without circumscription, above all things without any excluding position, it was not possible that he should be comprehended by the circumscribable human intellect, which uses the ministry of the senses for understanding, and that what is promised to it when purified at last in the homeland should be granted to it while confused and impure on the way.

But afterward, when our mind, the flesh at last left behind, has come forth clean, simple, pure, perfect, and consummated to its center, which is God, having been made equal to the angels, we shall know God perfectly, and all things, just as the holy Christ-bearer says to the Corinthians: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face.” For this reason we said that the angelic intellect, by the leading of nature, adheres immovably to its principle, because it is pure act and habit; since it is naturally simple in condition, it cannot be hindered by any commerce of composition. But the human intellect, as has now sufficiently been established and declared, since it is potency and privation, impure because of its commerce with its body, is indeed held back from perfect act until, at last freed from the flesh, it has passed into fellowship with the likeness of the angels, then for the first time to be admitted to the true knowledge of God. But if meanwhile the affect of love, necessary for salvation, is joined to present Christian faith and to future divine knowledge, the same everlasting blessedness with the holy angels is prepared as a gift for the worshipers of God. will be granted. But if a corrupted mind, through too much intercourse with its flesh, has despised the love of God, the intellect, once released from its prison, will indeed come forth, lofty in knowledge according to the measure belonging to it by nature; but it will be so much the more wretched, inasmuch as by its evil will it is found to be more like the demons. Therefore, to conclude the solution of the proposed question as far as I have been able: I say that it is not possible for almighty God to be perfectly understood by us as long as we live as mortals in the flesh.

On the Faith Necessary for Salvation.

Question Two

Question Second

The second question of your unconquered majesty was this: since today a small part of the world is subject to the laws of the Christian faith, whether that opinion of many people may be admitted without injury to truth, who think that each person, in his own religion which he believes to be true and saving, as a worshiper of the one God outside the Christian faith and without baptism, can be saved, provided that nothing is known of the religion of Christ.

To answer this question simply according to the common intention I have judged superfluous, since I know that today many among Christians, whom an impious piety on behalf of the salvation of lost people makes cruel in that very matter. But because the cause of just consideration stirred your most serene highness to ask these things, not because you do not know what must be held catholicly in this position, but so that you might have what truth to set against those who attack it, I shall answer the questions as briefly as I can. If anyone could be saved outside the Christian faith, Christ, the Son of almighty God, would seem to have been made man superfluously and without cause. For if there is salvation outside Christ, Christ is not the Savior of all. But because it was necessary, according to the Scriptures, that the only-begotten Son of God, for the salvation of the human race, should be born as a man in the world, suffer, die, and rise again on the third day, he did not come into this world in vain, nor superfluously, nor without cause. Since this is so, whoever asserts that anyone can be saved outside the faith of Christ shows himself not a Christian, but an adversary of the faith and a deserter of Christ. For whoever does not believe in Christ, the Son of God, promises himself eternal salvation in vain. For he himself, Jesus Christ, who is the Truth, says in the holy Gospel: “He who does not believe will be condemned.”

And again: “He who does not believe is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.” And again, a little later, he adds, saying: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Saint Christophylus also says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” The solution of the proposed question is now clear to all who truly believe in Christ: that salvation is through the Savior of the world himself, and whoever does not believe in him cannot be saved. Nor is it permitted for a Christian in any way to go beyond the bounds of his religion, so as to presume to explain this question otherwise than Christ taught. But whoever departs from this rule of faith by asserting the contrary is plainly shown not to think rightly concerning Christ, the Savior of the faithful. For whoever promises salvation to anyone outside Christ wishes to declare Christ a liar. But we, confirmed by the most sacred sanctions of the Gospel, firmly believe and pronounce without doubt that no one can be saved outside the faith of Christ, however much he may trust in his paternal religion or in another. Christ is salvation, and outside the Christian faith no one will be saved. For why did Christ, the Son of God, will to die for the sins of the world, if each person could have been saved outside faith in him, in his own paternal tradition? From the beginning of the world after the fall of the human race, it was impossible for anyone to be saved unto eternal life otherwise than in the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. What then if the greater part of mankind remains outside the faith of Jesus today? Did not the Savior of the world himself long ago foretell in the holy Gospel that many are called, but few are chosen? And again he says: “Enter through the narrow gate, for wide is the gate and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.” What can we say that contributes to God, our salvation, who has no need of our goods? For whether many are saved or many are damned, God himself is the unchangeable Lord of all. Nothing is added to him if all are saved; nothing is lacking if the whole world perishes. There is an infallible order of divine providence and majesty, which embraces those who are to be damned no less than those who are to be saved, each and all alike. No one No one who is to be damned certainly suffers injustice, since, just as we all fell in the first man, so no one is saved except in the blood of Jesus Christ through mercy, and no one is damned except in his own faithlessness and, according to his desert, through justice.

From the foregoing there arises another question, of no small difficulty, which human curiosity is accustomed to raise against those who think rightly concerning the faith of Christ. Why does almighty God, since he is just and merciful, not cease to create so many thousands of human beings whom he has most certainly foreknown are to be damned? Why does he not spare the wretched, and why does he bring forth into destruction, in such a multitude, those whom he has foreknown will turn aside to evil? For it would seem better not to exist than to exist badly.

Let him answer this question, if anyone thinks himself God’s counselor. Who am I, that I should expound the cause of the divine will? For whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, and there is no one who can resist his will. Hence a certain wise man says to God: Who will charge it against you if the nations that you made perish? The Almighty has established for things an order of vicissitude, which no fullness of change will ever revoke. B ij For just as he permits his sun to rise upon the good and the evil, so also, until the end of the age, he allows human beings to be conceived, born, and grow, the pious and the impious. The thoughts of human beings are not in God, nor does he change his counsel according to time; but since he is immutable and everlasting, willing all things together and once for all and always, he has from eternity unchangeably preordained them.

God speaks once, as sacred Scripture bears witness, and does not add, because whatever he wills he wills immovably, and he admits no change. Therefore, that human beings are born good and evil, pious and impious, faithful and faithless, sinners and saints, those to be saved and those to be damned, God permits by a most just reason, he who assigned this order to all things. Nothing is lost to God, who is Lord of all, and who firmly holds his rule everywhere no less over evil than over good human beings and spirits. Christ Jesus, God from God the Father without time, and man from the Virgin in time, appointed mediator of God and human beings, is himself the one through whom we have access to God. He is the savior of all the faithful, and whoever rashly grants that anyone can be saved without the Christian faith thinks wrongly concerning him.

The omnipotence of God has regard to the order of things that he established; according to its inviolable sequence of rectitude, no one will be saved without faith in Christ, and no one who does not believe in the Son of God is justified. Therefore those people are moved by empty and utterly foolish piety who think that someone outside the faith of Christ, in the whole world and in any sect whatever, is to be saved, when his own judgment is manifestly to the contrary. Let them hear the Savior himself again saying in the Gospel: No one comes to the Father except through me. For I am the way, the truth, and the life. If no one comes to the Father except through the Son, certainly no one will be saved except through him. Who will save the Jew and the pagan, when no one can be saved except through Christ? But Christ will undoubtedly save only those who believe in him with heart, speech, and deed. He will not save the Jew, not the Saracen, not the pagan, not any other unbeliever, because they do not believe in him, but despise his teaching, scorn the faith, and, blaspheming his holy name, revile it all day long. For he himself said in the Gospel: B 3 Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him I also shall be ashamed before my Father and his holy angels.

Tell me now, you who worship Christ and contend that someone can be saved outside the Christian faith in his own sect, which he thinks true. Do you believe the Gospel of Christ is true or false? If true, why do you think contrary to it? For Christ says that whoever has not believed in the Son of God, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he has already been judged and will be condemned, and that no one comes to the Father except through me. But you, led astray by I know not what rashness, thrust forward the contrary, saying that a person outside the faith of Christ, trusting in his paternal religion, which he believes to be true and to please God, or living innocently according to the law of nature, and especially since perhaps he has never heard anything of the faith of Christ, is to be saved in his confidence. Christ did not say this, but: whoever has believed in the only-begotten Son of God will be saved, but whoever has not believed will be condemned. He excepted no one, admitted no condition, because he who had come to suffer for all had provided for the salvation of all through faith alone. If faith 12 if faith in the Savior is lacking, then no confidence will save the unbeliever. For the holy bishop Augustine said in On Faith to Peter: “Hold most firmly, and do not doubt at all, that not only all pagans, but also all Jews, heretics, and schismatics who end this present life outside the Catholic Church will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

You see now where foolish compassion draws you: measuring God by human laws, so that you may make him merciful in all things, you do not fear to judge his only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, a liar. But Christ is truthful, who says that those who do not believe in him are to be condemned; you, however, are rash and false, who trust that anyone can be saved outside his faith. Whoever truly believes in Christ does not allow anyone at all outside the unity of the Catholic Church of Christians to be called saved. Whoever says the contrary shows that he is not a true and good Christian. For this is the inviolable judgment of Catholic tradition, which the Lord Jesus himself, the Son of God, defined in the holy Gospel: namely, that no one is to be saved outside his faith, which he himself established, taught, and confirmed by his own blood. Therefore whoever affirms that a person is to be saved in any sect whatever outside the faith of Jesus Christ, or believes it in his heart, is not a good Christian, but rather an apostate and a disciple of Antichrist; and unless he comes to his senses, let him know that he will be tormented forever in hell with him. For he who says that one who does not believe in the Lord Jesus is to be saved without the Savior is not a Christian, but an Antichrist.

Therefore, most wise Caesar, let no one appear in the sight of your Majesty, let no one feel that you adhere to him, who thinks that people are to be saved outside the faith of Jesus Christ. For everyone who believes that anyone is to be saved outside the faith of Christ has denied both Christ and his Gospel. But when we say that all who are not Christians are to be condemned, this is not a sign of cruelty, but of true piety. For it is better to believe the truth firmly than to consent falsely to a man. That all Jews, pagans, gentiles, Saracens, schismatics, heretics, and unbelievers are without doubt to be damned eternally with the demons is attested by the Church of the saints, which took and confirmed this judgment from no other source than Christ’s words.

13 For thus he said: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life,” by which good Christians in faith and work are designated. “But he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Here all Jews, pagans, Saracens, gentiles, and all who do not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ are denoted.

Concerning schismatics and heretics, the judgment of Christ is plain in the Gospel when he says: “If he refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican.” Gentiles are heathens, and publicans are manifest and public sinners; concerning their most certain damnation the Church of the saints has no doubt. For what Christian would doubt that gentiles and monstrous, manifest sinners are to be damned? Therefore, since all schismatics and heretics despise the Church of the saints, they are most rightly said to be like the gentiles and publicans who are to be condemned for their offenses and deserts, and they will justly undergo equal punishments of everlasting damnation with them.

Behold those whom the just sentence of Christ the Savior has condemned: foolish human compassion, not to say impious cruelty, presumes that they are to be saved. They desire, toward ruined people, to be merciful to ruined men, and they do not fear to show themselves cruel toward God. Those whom he, by justice, has assigned to death, they assert, with the worst presumption, should be called back to life. It is neither good nor useful for a Christian, whether seriously or in jest, to contradict Christ. He is impious, not Christian, whoever says that unbelievers are to be saved. In Adam, the first man, when he fell, we all sinned, and the wrath of God remained over the whole human race from the beginning of the world until Christ. Christ came, born of the Virgin; being God and man, innocent of sin, he voluntarily underwent the death of the cross, and, having been made mediator between God and man, removed the wrath of original guilt from those who believe in him. For thus he says: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life. But he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Indeed, without faith in Jesus Christ no one will be saved, however justly and holily he may seem to live in his own religion. For almighty God can save a believer without material baptism, but he cannot make a denier saved without faith. No one is saved unwillingly, because no one believes except willingly. For the Lord knows those who are his, since he saves those who believe in the Son through penitence, but condemns unbelievers through the equity of justice.

From this, a new question, having come in between, struck my mind: what should be thought about the infants and simple-minded persons of unbelieving pagans and Jews? To this a brief answer must be given. Just as the infants of Christians, baptized in the faith of their parents, are saved, so the children of all unbelievers, not baptized, will be damned in the unbelief of their parents. The judgment is similar concerning simple-minded persons of either religion: just as we believe without doubt that baptized simple-minded persons among Christians are saved, so we should say without doubt that those of unbelievers are damned. Again, it is asked here what should be thought, in a Catholic sense, about those people who inhabit the islands newly discovered in the great sea, of which there is no mention among the ancient cosmographers, and who, as we have been informed, have never heard anything at all about the Christian religion. A brief answer is given, conforming in every respect to what has been set out above: truth has wholly excepted no unbeliever from damnation, no islander, no one adjacent to our world, no one else at all, whether dwelling near or far away, but includes them without distinction and without definition of persons, saying: “He who has believed and has been baptized will be saved; but he who has not believed will be condemned,” and the wrath of God remains upon him. Who removes the wrath of God from man, except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mediator of God and men? By what means, except through faith formed in him who, innocent, tasted death? Since, therefore, no one is saved without faith, we cannot promise salvation to those ignorant of Christ, whom it is clear do not have the devotion of faith in him. And so we must necessarily say that all who do not believe in the Son of God are to be damned, whether they have heard of him or are wholly ignorant of him.

Yet we concede one thing: if any among those who are ignorant of Christ lived well according to the law of nature, calling upon one God, even if they sometimes sinned, provided they had done penance before death, they have been or will be damned less gravely than those who either hear of Christ and despise him, or who, among either group, lived wickedly and sordidly. For God is just, and does injury to no one, but repays each according to his works. But the wrath of God remains upon upon everyone who does not believe in his only-begotten Son, because of the original sin of the first man, from which no one is justified except through faith and the baptism of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. But if original sin is in a person alone, as in little children, unless it is removed through Christ it condemns the one who has it only to the punishment of loss, namely, by which he is shut out from the vision of God and from the enjoyment of the blessedness of the saints forever. But an adult who sins mortally will be punished after death with a double punishment, namely of loss and of sense, so that he does not see God, and, feeling the pains of the fire of Gehenna without end, never escapes. Jews, Saracens, and all the rest who, hearing the faith of Christ, despise it are without doubt damned to both punishments, of loss and of sense, whether otherwise they live innocently according to the law of nature or the contrary. But among those who have never had any hearing of Christ, if any lived innocently according to the law of nature until death, I do not think they have provided cause for being said or believed to be damned to the punishment of sense, although they are deprived forever of the vision of God, which theologians have called the punishment of loss.

For no one will behold the face of God the almighty Father unless he has been reborn through faith in Christ. Now let us settle the judgment against those who, while we assert these things according to the catholic doctrine of Christ, are prompted by foolish reflection to object: Why did almighty God, since he is supremely good, will to create so many thousands of human beings whom he foreknew from eternity were to be damned? For if Christians are compared with unbelievers, scarcely a twentieth part of the people of the whole world today believes in our Lord Jesus Christ.

The boundless curiosity of this question has often troubled many people; if their faith in Christ were firm, and devotion fervent in them with love, they would not ask such unusual and difficult things. For what man of such learning or holiness is found among mortals that, apart from God himself, he could disclose to us the cause of the divine will? For the cause of God’s will is incomprehensible, since he himself is the cause of his most righteous will. The eternal order is inviolable; and, as I said above, God does injury to no one. When God brought the universal flood upon the earth, were not only eight people saved in the ark?

All the rest perished by the inundation of the waters. The cause of their perishing was sin; but that they were created had no other cause than the uncircumscribable goodness of God. Because few are saved while many perish, the figure preceded the mystery: the ark of Noah was the sacrament of the Christian faith. For just as all outside Noah’s ark perished in the flood, so now all who are outside the unity of the catholic Church of Christians will without doubt perish forever in their sins: Jews as well as pagans, heretics together with schismatics. The justice of God damns those whom goodness created. Mercy, however, saves those whom grace has confirmed, because, as the holy Apostle says, “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” since “he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.” Let us weigh rightly the freedom of the human will, and we shall know the just will of God.

Concerning the Miracles of Unbelievers. Third Question.

Question Third

The third question of your most serene Majesty was: If no one is saved outside the faith, whence come miracles among unbelievers, since we have learned by the report of many that astonishing things are done even among unbelievers?

The solution of this question, as it seems to me, will not be difficult if we apply faith to the Scriptures and the necessary consideration to the natural powers of the soul. A miracle is a new and unusual event, which happens outside customary practice and draws human beings into wonder. Hence good Christians, bad Christians, and unbelievers work miracles in different ways. Good Christians indeed work miracles through public justice; bad Christians through the signs of public justice; but unbelievers through private contracts with demons, whether implicit or explicit. Concerning the good, the Lord said in the holy Gospel: “These signs will follow those who have believed: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new tongues; they will take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands upon the sick, and they will be well.” But concerning bad Christians who work miracles in the name of Jesus Christ, we read written thus in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons? And in your name did we not do many mighty works?”

“And then I will confess to them: I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity.” But outside the Church of God, where the name of our Lord Jesus Christ is not invoked, if any wonders are done beyond the custom of nature or human art, no good Christian doubts that they are done by the cooperation of demons. And your Caesar’s serenity, with discernment of virtue, judges works of this kind as deserving to be called wonders rather than miracles. Nor does this judgment of truth depart from reason, insofar as a necessary distinction should be maintained between prodigies of light and of darkness. I find four agents of wonders; but I recognize one only who truly works miracles, God, principally as the cause of all good things. Therefore the first and greatest agent of all marvelous things is God, who filled and illuminated the whole world with signs, miracles, and powers. None of the others is to be compared with him: he created heaven and earth, the sea and all things that are in them; he alone is omnipotent, just, holy and upright, good, incomprehensible, greatest, glorious, immense, and eternal. All other things are beneath him, since whatever in this world is marvelously able can happen, is certainly less than the whole world itself, which he was able to create out of nothing. Likewise, every miracle that can be done through a human being is less than the human being himself, whom God, the creator of all things, formed from the beginning in his own image and likeness. And although God’s miracles among visible natures now almost grow cheap among mortals because of the constant sight of them, nevertheless, if we look upon them wisely, they will appear to all greater and rarer than any unusual things.

The manner, however, in which God works miracles is the unchangeable will of God, which, since it is omnipotent, does whatever it has wished in heaven and on earth. For he himself spoke, and they were made; he himself commanded, and they were created. The will of God is ordered and everlasting; therefore his miracles are incomparably greater than the rest. For greater than all the miracles of this world is what we behold: the whole universe, and whatever is contained in it, created by the will of God. The divine will, unchangeably enduring, works all things, since it lacks both beginning and end; but whatever God wills, he always wills, because, since willing and being able are the same in him, there is no labor for the unchangeable one. Hence all the universal miracles which the creator of all things performs, he has set forth for both good and evil persons to behold; and after the general miracles, which have now become cheap among mortals through use, he has also shown, in almost every individual creature, infinitely many special wonders.

The second worker of miracles is the good angel, who very often performs wondrous things for mortals both by natural power and by divine authority. For those most blessed spirits are sent, by divine ordinance, into ministry for the faithful; and they furnish to both good and evil persons the benefits that belong to nature, but to those alone who believe in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ they administer the gifts of saving grace. Hence there is no doubt that those miracles which occur through invocation of the divine name in the Church of the saints are displayed by the ministry and cooperation of those same angels.

But the wonders of unbelievers, if any either occur today or are read to have been done long ago, are either fabricated, or falsely claimed, or are carried out by the deception of demons. For it cannot happen that any unbelievers work miracles by the ministry of good angels, since where Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is not believed in, no signs of grace are displayed through good spirits to impious and reprobate human beings. For indeed, since they are obstinate in the error of a false religion, if they have attained anything miraculous in their own estimation, it must by no means be doubted that it is done through the ministry of demons. For since they are altogether unlike the good angels, they obtain no fellowship with them. Nor can any despiser of the Christian faith please God; but whatever is shown to displease almighty God is undoubtedly deprived of the fellowship of the holy angels.

Yet by this we do not take back the claim that every human being is entrusted to some good spirit, by whose ministry, even if he is an unbeliever in the Son of God, he may receive the benefits of nature, although he does not reach the gifts of grace. But to those who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, they confer not only the benefits of nature, but also administer the gifts of grace.

It is therefore clear that if any miracles occur among unbelievers, they cannot occur by the gift of God or by the ministry of the holy angels, since all such people are placed outside the unity of the Church, and the impious cannot work signs by public righteousness. For God, as has been said, does not remove his original wrath from a human being except through faith in Jesus Christ; but everyone who is unbelieving toward the Son of God will not see eternal life, but the wrath of God remains 19 remains upon him. Therefore everyone upon whom the wrath of God remains will not be able to please God; and therefore, if any wonders are done at his prayers, they should be believed to have been brought about not by the power of God nor by the ministry of angels, but rather by the interposition of demons.

The third effector of wonders is the devil, who, like an ape, longs to imitate whatever he has seen, and deceives the minds of men, especially unbelievers, with various illusions, and seduces those who believe him by a certain likeness of miracles. For I do not judge it difficult for demons to be able to mock the senses of men, since it is agreed that by nature they were created subtler than all mortals. But they cannot know the thoughts of mortals except by a kind of conjecture, namely when we make our inner thoughts manifest by certain signs. Demons foretell future things, and sometimes they speak truths, while sometimes they are deceived in their conjectures and mislead. From the beginning of the world they have known certain signs that precede an event; by experience and use of these, they sometimes foretell truly what is to come, since when they have seen signs known to them as preceding the event, they immediately infer what is in a man’s thought. C. 3 Yet more often they deceive, because they themselves are deceived. For when they are questioned about some matter that they do not know, as, for example, whether a messenger sent far away will return soon, or on what day, they immediately, in the blink of an eye, arrive at the place where they know him to be. When they have seen that he has already begun the journey to return, they carefully count the days, and, having suddenly returned to the questioner, they affirm that on a definite day the absent man will come. But if he has either delayed on the road or turned aside elsewhere, then the demons, deceived in their judgment, must necessarily be mistaken. They willingly mix themselves into prophecies, and are quite ready to predict future things to men for the sake of honor and esteem, since they greatly desire to be regarded as worthy of admiration, they seek divine honors, and they strongly desire to be feared by mortals. Just as boys hiding in secret places, or running about in masks, suddenly burst out from their hiding places and shake their companions, who suspect no such thing, with unexpected terror, and then hide themselves again lest they be recognized; and when they look upon the terrified men who do not know, they boast of the honor, as though they seem to have attained something great from this.

20 Some demons, after their example, are more fixed to the earth and, being those who move about among men, are excessively restless; the ancients called them bacucci. They terrify men at night and seek nothing more from mortals than the esteem of divinity. Hence also, before those with whom they are permitted to be by reason of similarity, they sometimes perform various tricks, and present themselves as terrifying to their minds, as chance may allow. As often as they can, they gladly put on the likeness of a human body; but they do not always find a suitable material of air with which to be clothed. Therefore they more often appear monstrous and horrible, because they have not had suitable humors or vapors for the perfection of the appearance they desired. But the more they are fixed to earthly dwellings, the duller they have become by descent toward matter. Hence, because of the ignorance that they have contracted through disobedience, the predictions of demons are frequently false, although by divine permission they are also sometimes verified. For as that most holy John Chrysostom says: It has been granted to the devil sometimes to speak the truth, so that he may commend his lie by a rare truth, because if never if he were to speak the truth, he could deceive no one, and his seduction would by no means suffice for temptation. It is therefore no wonder if demons sometimes seem to foretell true things to unbelieving people, since they were once able to produce prophecies in idols among the gentiles. Nor is it any wonder if they sometimes provide treatment for the sick, since they know the natures of all herbs and can very readily apply them to the sick, and either remove diseases that they had previously inflicted, or for a time withdraw from the senses the afflictions that mischance has imposed. For almighty God, by the right of his imperial majesty over all things, uses even the ministry of demons, both for the testing of the faithful and for the punishment of the impious. Since they are perverse in affection, obstinate in their rebellion, and proud, they especially desire divine esteem and honors; and therefore they gladly come to the invocations that unbelievers are accustomed to pour out to their gods, as though they themselves were gods. Among unbelievers they sometimes seem to restore the dead to life, and they show marvelous things to curious men, so that, as if by miracles, they may make them thoroughly confirmed and altogether obstinate in their former error. Yet they do not truly raise the dead, but deceive human senses in various ways: either they themselves enter the corpses of the dead and carry them about for a time as though alive, or, after those bodies have been removed to a more distant place, they present to the onlookers some likeness in the form of the departed person's life to be seen, as the experience of certain men has informed us. We believe it manifest that demons can display, in a certain false likeness, all the things that the saints perform as true miracles. All the miracles of demons are either phantasms or things done by a certain natural skill. For if men experienced in the more hidden mysteries of nature, by applying matter to form in a way obscure to others, produce unusual and marvelous effects, such as forming natural eels from the dew of heaven, bees from calves' flesh, serpents from certain roots of herbs, and many things like these, not to mention greater ones, as proof has made us experienced in very many cases, who would deny that demons, being of a subtler nature and greater experience, can naturally perform more marvelous things that are manifest to no human beings?

The fourth worker of miracles is man, who works marvelous things in four ways, things which, to those who do not know either the cause or the manner, do not seem human. First, indeed, by invocation of the divine name, when in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ the merit of accepted holiness concurs. In this way the holy apostles and their imitators worked miracles by the power of God and at the same time by the merit of holiness, in the unity of faith. But unbelievers cannot work miracles in this way, for they do not walk the necessary path of faith toward salvation. For even if many of them believe in one God, nevertheless, because they refuse to believe in the mediator between God and human beings, they have been driven very far away from God's mercy. But with the holy Gospel promising it, all things are possible for those who believe in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, for those who also adorn right faith with holy works. For just as without faith it is impossible to please God, so also faith without works is dead. Almighty God would grant us all the things that we ask in the faith of Christ, if we did all the things that we ought according to faith. Believe firmly and act faithfully, and you will always obtain all things.

Second, man works miracles through the likeness of angelic purity. For when our mind, confirmed in the faith of Jesus Christ, has become purer through love, then, having been made more like the holy angels, it attains greater familiarity with them. But whoever has attained complete familiarity with the holy angels will, whenever he wishes, shine forth in miracles by God's gift. For the holy angels reveal to pure men who are fervent in the love of God secrets hidden from others, and by command of the Creator they make many things manifest to them. For the Lord is near to those who call upon him in truth. The Lord will do the will of those who fear him; he will hear their prayers and save them. For whoever is one with Christ through grace is refreshed by the frequent visitation of angels, and often, when necessity requires, is made illustrious by signs and mighty works through their ministry. Hence it is that even those oppressed by various illnesses betake themselves to the intercession of the saints, and, turning over in their mind the Lord's promises, obtain by others' merits what they cannot obtain by their own. Their holy devotion in the faith of Christ receives the salvation of the Lord, since, assisted both by the purity of their own conscience and supported by the merit of another's holiness, it is not rashly borne up into sure hope.

...it does not rashly arise. Miracles occur in the Church of God by divine power in three respects or through three means. Sometimes almighty God works a miracle through the ministry of angels, solely by the merits of the one who performs it, just as Saint Martin healed the blind man and the lame man against their will. Sometimes miracles occur solely by the merit of the sufferer, as we read that many were cured through bad Christians, whom the sick believed to be excellent in faith. Third, there is no doubt that healings of this kind occur by the merit of both, that is, of the sufferer and the performer together, as Christ says to a certain person in the holy Gospel: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.” For faith is always required for a miracle, so that our Lord Jesus Christ, coming into his own country, marveled that he could perform no mighty work there because of their unbelief. But none of these things is done among unbelievers, where neither holiness is found in the working nor orthodox faith in the sufferer.

Third, therefore, a human being performs miracles through the mediation of cooperation with diabolical wickedness, and this can happen in three ways: namely by manifest invocation of demons, by implication, and by substitution.

By manifest invocation necromancers and the women whom we commonly call witches perform marvelous things; depraved by similarity of will, they have passed into fellowship with demons. For just as in the Church of God the sacraments are signs of the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, so in the school of demons certain characters and modes of invocation are signs of a pact between a human being and a malignant spirit. Hence malignant spirits, when invoked, have gladly been accustomed to come to those who display the signs of demons, and to exhibit dreadful malefices together with certain marvelous things. But witches and necromancers produce marvelous effects by the invocation of demons in different ways. Witches are subjected to demons by a kind of profession; by their ministry they disturb the air, raise storms, devastate crops, weaken human beings and beasts of burden, carry on foul commerce of the filthiest pleasure with demons, and by pernicious spells recall from the lower world into sight whomever they wish. Their deeds should not be called miracles, but rather malefices, and deservedly punished by the most extreme penalty. Necromancers, however, subject themselves to demons not by a manifest profession, but by an implicit condition, when they promise that they can compel them to appear visibly within a circle, not only by conjurations and the display of characters, but also by sacrifices, fumigations, and vows. Their crimes are without number, since it is manifest that they all conspire, either implicitly or explicitly, into fellowship with demons. Although necromancers are not all equal either in art or in work, nevertheless, to their own destruction, they are all united in damnable curiosity, by which they desire, with the help of a demon, to obtain what they cannot discover naturally. All their works and books are full of superstitions and impiety, and for that reason must be driven far from the borders of believers.

There is a great multitude of enchanters and necromancers in the East, who by their illusions miserably deceive the human race, and have turned almost all of Asia, greater and lesser, away from the faith of Christ. Illusions can occur in three ways: by the ministry of demons, by the operation of nature, and by the deception of human art. No true Christian will doubt that the miracles of unbelievers occur in one of these ways, when the root of the worker has been set down as determinate. But today there are commonly...

24 There are today many among Christians devoted to the works of demons: enchanters, evildoers, and persons reprobate with respect to the faith, who deceive many through excessive curiosity and promise impossibilities by their arts.

By the involvement of demons, moreover, wondrous things sometimes occur: namely, whenever a person not firmly enough established in the faith does or desires something otherwise than befits a Christian, even if he believes it to be no sin. Since this ought not to be done, the devil nevertheless intrudes and often supplies the desired effect. Such, indeed, is that practice which convulsives commonly use. On the holy day of Parasceve they make, during the office, a ring of whatever metal, which the person thereafter always wears on the heart-finger. These things are utterly empty and have no root of truth at all. Yet I cannot deny that I have seen some people cured of spasm by this same emptiness.

Likewise, I know that certain people have opened very strong locks with words and herbs; I judge that this was done neither by the power of God nor by the force of the things applied. I could introduce countless similar things that I have seen and heard; what are their manifest effects other than certain miracles of demons?

There are, finally, some excessively curious people who stubbornly place faith and confidence in characters, written slips, rings, figures, necklaces, and unknown words, and often attain wondrous effects. We do not at all doubt that the devil has supplied these, not by the merit of holiness nor by the mercy granted by God, but rather through faithless credulity. For demons, having the greatest envy of the human race and wishing to destroy the souls of mortals, gladly come to meet the empty operations of the impious. What, indeed, are characters and interpretations of hidden names other than certain foods and drinks of demons? Whoever places faith in characters that promise wondrous effects has implicitly denied both the faith of Christ and the Church of the saints.

Alas, how many Christians today, how many clerics, how many priests, to spare their superiors, use many and various superstitions in their daily actions; by these they follow entangled pacts of demons, to the dishonor of the Christian faith and their own condemnation. And because these evils have now multiplied too greatly among Christians, the Almighty has withdrawn his hand and has handed them over into the dominion of the faithless, so that they may feel as punishers of their penalties those in imitation of whom they stubbornly served, not the living and true God, but empty superstitions.

If we examine the truth more diligently, we plainly recognize that wondrous things are done by the supposition of demons. For if Jews, Saracens, pagans, or gentiles, who do not believe in our God Jesus Christ, perform any miracles, we believe that this is done not by the power of God, not by the ministry of angels, not by the merit of holiness, but by the supposition of demons. For whenever they invoke almighty God, in whose only-begotten Son they do not believe, for the merciful granting of some wondrous effect, the devil, knowing that there is no salvation for sinners and that the Most High does not hear unbelieving sinners, secretly applies himself in place of the God invoked, so that he may preserve them obstinate in their errors; and, if he can, with the Lord permitting it, he supplies to those praying what is requested. The devil uses this supposition the more freely, the less he is impeded by the faith of Christ and the sacraments of the Church. For the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers who do not believe in his only-begotten Son, and they are in the power of the devil; and therefore he insinuates himself in the place of God to those who invoke him. Hence, blinded in their errors, they invoke God, in whose Son they do not believe; when he despises hearing them as they remain under wrath, the devil, the false worker of miracles, approaches. Therefore those who scorn believing the true miracles of God believe in the devil’s mockeries. Those who refused to follow the truth, that is, Christ, by believing, receive from demons false miracles suited to their errors.

For among unbelievers there are many who worship one God, the creator of all things, do not adore idols, and firmly believe that they will be saved in their own faith. But because they despise believing the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the wrath of God remains upon them, and they vanish away in their follies. Thinking that God is near to them, though they do not believe rightly in him, they are subjected to demons; by placing faith in their false miracles, they are confirmed by a lie in their errors.

It will not be irksome, Caesar, to introduce a likeness of this matter. There was a certain swineherd who had enclosed in the staff used for his pigs a written slip containing the name of the holy martyr Blaise. He attributed so much faith to it that, when the staff was fixed in the ground in the middle of the herd, lu...that he believed every wolf was kept from approaching. When this foolish confidence had at last been strengthened by long experience, the man went securely wherever he wished, leaving the pigs in the wood without danger, since now no wolf had any access to them. It happened that a seer passed by while the shepherd was absent; seeing that a demon was keeping guard over the herd, he said to him, “Wretch, what are you doing here?” He answered, “I am guarding these pigs.” The other said, “Who entrusted the care of the pigs to you?” He answered again, “The foolish confidence of the shepherd. For he has sinned against his own law, believing that a certain slip enclosed in a staff has the power of great piety, by which, through the merits of some Blaise, wolves are kept away from the pigs, and he follows our vanities. But because the one invoked does not appear, I, lest the man lose his confidence, guard his pigs and willingly substitute myself for Blaise.” Thus, he said, mortals trouble us with vain conjurations, so that, unless we wish to lose all estimation of ourselves and honor among them, we must very often come to meet their foolish invocations. By the likeness of this deed, demons deceive merciful unbelievers, and the miracles that they request from God in prayer they quite often obtain through the substitution of malignant spirits.

For demons gladly insert themselves into those matters that concern either the worship or the honor of God; and those who cannot obtain manifest honors are indeed greatly delighted by hidden ones. At the same time it must be noted that, from the beginning of the world, miracles have never been lacking to any religion or sect of principal excellence, although not all were done from one source. For whatever miracles have been done in the true religion have been done from no source other than God. The law of nature had its miracles, the written law had them, and now grace likewise has them. Almighty God, who gave religion, himself also performs miracles. But in false religions, where truth is not worshiped, if any miracles are performed, it is not God but the devil who works them.

For since God is truth, he did not institute false religions, and therefore he has never adorned a lie with his miracles. Muhammad, who, full of an evil demon, instituted a false religion, adorned it with false miracles not from God but by the cooperation of demons. For the demon who gave the cause of the error could also, when an occasion had been accepted, display a false miracle to the deceived. Hence, if miracles had been wholly lacking to Muhammad as he persuaded an untaught people to accept a new religion, perhaps no one would have put faith in him. For he himself also showed certain wonders to the peoples, both by subtlety of intellect and by the cooperation of the devil, so that he might seem to have confirmed a new doctrine with new miracles as well. Miracles were not lacking even to idolatrous pagans, if we do not deny trust to the histories. The Jews, however, before the incarnation of the Son of God, receiving his law through Moses, were frequently illuminated by divine miracles. But after the Lord’s resurrection, when the Mosaic law had been made void, those who do not believe in the only-begotten Son of God remain under the wrath of his indignation, and all miracles of truth have ceased among them. Hence if they do any wonders today, they are works of demons and manifest judgments of error. For demons watch with the greatest zeal so that those men whom they have once made to wander from the way of truth, which is Christ, they may, by a continuation of fraud, make obstinate in error until death. Indeed, when God withdraws his grace from unbelievers by a just reckoning, their deceiver, the malignant spirit, approaches unknown; and when he sees that salvation is far away, by false miracles he deceives the minds of the ignorant, as though the Lord were near.

...leads them astray. Therefore whatever miracles occur among unbelievers are works of demons, since just as there is no salvation for mortals outside the unity of the Christian faith, so without Christ the most holy power of wonders is not granted. For now demons, lurking in their snares, long ago conquered and confounded by the trophy of Christ, fear to appear openly as they did before the incarnation of the Lord; and therefore among unbelievers they falsely present themselves as good spirits.

There are also some who add a fourth mode to the three already described, saying that the mind, or spirit, of the human being himself can naturally work marvels, provided that he knows how to recall himself from every adventitious thing into himself, above sense, into unity. For those who maintain such things promise marvels of nature: to predict the future, disclose people’s secrets, remove diseases, and suddenly change people’s plans. But this mode of miracles cannot be simply natural, certain, common, and infallible, since, if it is true, which I have not experienced, some external power must necessarily already come into play and occupy the thought in part, whether a good angel or a malignant spirit. But if none of the external powers intervenes,

then the person prophesying must necessarily form the basis of his speech either from conjectures or from bold presumption, and pronounce a judgment sometimes true and sometimes false. Indeed, so long as the spirit dwells in the body, it naturally understands nothing without the ministry of sense. Hence I would not wholly resist if they conceded that our confused and untrained intellect is assisted by a similar ministry.

For we see among those who, very often in the desire of inward love for Jesus, transcend the measure of the flesh in contemplation, that they are lifted upward from the earth into the air; and we think that they exceed bodily weight not only by their own keenness of mind, but also by divine power. Therefore three principles of the opinion already mentioned, unknown to many, are enough in my judgment for a few cases: that the mind, while placed in the body, should by its own power work marvelous effects outside itself.

What then? Let anyone ignorant of nature tell me whether bodily weight can be lightened by the operation of the mind. With two men bearing witness together with me, I say that this is a thing experienced. When as a young man I was pursuing the study of letters, four of us were sleeping one night in one bed. A companion of my own age rose from my side, and while asleep, as he was accustomed,

in dreams, with his eyes closed and the moon shining inside, almost as if awake, walked around the house. He climbed walls and overcame the window by his agility. Sleeping, he also crossed over the bed a second and third time, stepped on all of us with his feet, and we felt no greater weight than if a tiny mouse had touched us. Wherever his sleeping body moved, all the fastenings of the doors opened of their own accord at once. He passed through the higher parts of the house very swiftly, and clung to the roofs in the manner of a sparrow.

I am speaking of what I saw, not of things heard by wandering report. These seem to be functions of the soul, not of the body; the soul, by its own natural power, so to speak, uses them almost freely when, with the senses of the flesh bound, it wanders outside the dwelling-place of the body. But since this matter does not fit the proposed question in every respect, let us defer the discussion of the causes of these marvels to another time. For we do not think these things marvelous to the wise, who have understood very well the power and nobility of the human mind, inasmuch as, hindered only by the interposition of the body, it is otherwise judged equal to the angels. Finally, we pass over the various modes and kinds of fascinations, by which, for outward effects, a frenzied person produces marvelous works.

29 ...produces effects. A very strongly confident imagination also has much power to produce marvelous effects, whether it is directed toward a real object or toward one merely supposed. Therefore, since there are so many kinds and modes of working marvels, it is no wonder if Jews, Saracens, pagans, gentiles, and all others placed outside the faith of Christ, unbelievers who cannot work miracles through public righteousness, accomplish marvels either by the aid of demons or by artful industry. Nor does it escape me that by the same reasoning the miracles of the saints are attacked by the impious, as though they were not by the power of the Creator but rather by the involvement or substitution of the devil. Whoever truly believes that the Christian faith alone is true does not doubt that all the miracles of unbelievers are performed by the cooperation of demons. But if anyone rashly and stubbornly thinks the contrary, he shows himself to be an unbeliever, not a Christian.

On Sacred Scripture, the Fourth Question.

Question Fourth

The fourth question of your most serene majesty was this: Why almighty God did not give holy Scripture, containing the mysteries of our faith in both the New and the Old Testament, open, manifest, uniform in all things, and plainly sufficient for everything, but rather wrapped up and, in many places, full of riddles. For many things necessary to the perfection of faith are not found sufficiently expressed in the divine Scriptures. To this question of your most sacred majesty, it seems that one should respond as follows. Every Scripture divinely inspired is a perfect work of divinity, ordained before all time, written in time, not otherwise than God willed, who inspired human beings so that it might be written. All God’s works are perfect; and therefore, since the Scripture of which we are speaking is God’s work, it is necessary to acknowledge it as perfect in all things. For the supreme judge, God, whose works are all perfect, gave to his Scriptures the order he willed and as he willed, and without doubt infused into those who received them the manner in which they were to write. For almighty God gave so much authority and majesty to sacred Scripture that, in comparison with it, all the words of this world fail, since divine things cannot properly be comprehended by human speech.

Therefore divine Scripture, which on the surface of its words appears confused to the ignorant, seems manifest to those who know it, because unless it is read by that Spirit by which it is believed to have been infused into human beings, one by no means comes to understand it.

The learned man who burns under the shadow of the flesh with vain desires reads it in one way, and the understanding man, whom the love of God truly inflames after he has been stripped of pleasures, reads it in another. Hence it is no wonder if human beings who are wise in a fleshly way do not understand the divine Scriptures: blinded by the pleasures of the flesh, they have never perceived the sweetness of God’s Spirit. It is as if you were to show any written volume to a boy learning the first elements of letters, whose script differed from his own little book; when he could not read the writing, he would immediately cry out that it was bad and not correctly formed. In the same way, people who approach the reading of the divine Scriptures with only fleshly wisdom, who do not grasp the things that belong to the divine Spirit, weighed down by vices and rashness, when they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, instead criticize the holy Scriptures which they do not understand. For it is not permitted to everyone indiscriminately to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest the beast touching the mountain be overwhelmed with stones. Now many rise up in a backward order, who have spent the whole time of their life on the literature of the humanities, and, having become old men, wrongly interpreting the divine Scriptures which they never learned, they do not clarify them but confuse them, and discuss them according to their own understanding. Hence all who do not understand the sacred Scriptures by the Spirit by which they were infused into those who wrote them have the veil of ignorance and rashness spread over their hearts, like the Jews; and from that source they often draw the poison of pernicious error, from which humble people approaching in the Spirit of God have received the cup of salvation. For heavenly teaching is not held in the words of the Scriptures but in the meaning; not on the surface of speech, but in the understanding; not in the leaves of ornate discourse, but in the hidden place of mystical inspiration. Hence Saint Pope Gregory says: Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in its manner of speaking, since in one and the same discourse, while it narrates the text, it discloses a hidden mystery; and just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise with mystery. For it has publicly that from which it may nourish little ones.

31 and keeps hidden that by which it may suspend the minds of the lofty in admiration of its sweetness, like a certain marvelous river in which both a simple little lamb may walk and a great elephant may swim. And Saint Augustine says on Genesis: Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth it terrifies the attentive, by its power it feeds the great, and by its affability it nourishes little ones. For the authority of sacred Scripture is greater than all the keenness of human intellect. Therefore, in order that one may arrive at their true understanding, first the mind must be purged of every carnal affection, and the aid of divine goodness must be diligently implored with humility, so that by his Spirit he may illumine the understanding of the learner. For the necks of all powers must be submitted to the authority of the divine Scriptures; and, as Saint Jerome says, one must never flatter any person in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected. That truth, in both Testaments, is wholly true in its narration of deeds, right in its admonitions, certain in its promises, and terribly to be feared in its threats. Therefore it has not been granted to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but this is permitted only to those, insofar as it is permitted at all, for whom love maintains continuous study and the Spirit of God grants true understanding to purified minds. But whoever is filthy with the darkness of vices, whoever walks proudly with a swollen mind, whoever doubts the truth of God’s Scriptures either in part or as a whole, should never trust that he can reach an understanding of them. For the authority of Scripture itself says: unless you have believed, you will not understand. It is due to the slowness of our intellect, and also to the impurity of our desire, whenever we do not rightly understand the divine Scriptures, namely when the veil of pernicious occupation remains spread over our hearts, which does not allow us to arrive at true understanding. Hence it happens that we do not understand the sense which the Holy Spirit infused into the divine Scriptures, but, seizing on the bare words of the writers, twist them into another sense. Indeed, if our minds were purified from carnal vices, if the intellect were exercised in the Scriptures through the continual pursuit of sobriety, if that belief and reverence were applied to the holy Scriptures which their dignity requires, every studious person would understand more clearly than light that there is nothing confused in sacred readings, nothing discordant, nothing unfitting, nothing absurd, or inserted without a most just reason. Indeed, all passages of divine Scripture are full of mysteries; and whenever something in them seems to have been set down obscurely, this was done by divine providence, so that the studious mind might have the necessary exercise of piety, and the faith of the simple, with due reverence, might not lose its place. Therefore it was not by chance, but by eternal providence, that he willed the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that they might abound in so many mysteries; and this, with the Spirit of God inspiring them, is explained in a catholic manner by teachers. For, as sacred Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is useful and greatly profitable, because it gives birth to many meanings of truth and brings them forth into the light for human beings; for when one person draws out this sense and another that sense by expounding it in a catholic manner, how lofty and profound Scripture is becomes known. Therefore let no person swollen with secular literature suppose that he understands sacred Scripture, unless he has first laid aside the veil of pride and of every disordered desire. For secular learning has greater power to exercise the intellect than to illuminate the understanding for true wisdom. Therefore divine Scripture is without doubt clear and bright to purified minds, to those for whom there is continual exercise in the fear of God and frequent zeal for reading, though to the filthy and to those puffed up with secular wisdom it seems confused and obscure. Hence that person understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly who, with purified affection and frequent in the study of them, expounds them as did the one who wrote them.
