For if they are read in a spirit other than that by which he is believed to have inspired them to be written, the mind must necessarily be wholly barred from true understanding. But when we encounter some dissonance in them, we should understand that it belongs only to the words and not to the meanings; and this arises in an ordered way not by chance, but by the providence of God, so that the mind, exercised longer in the Scriptures, may be strengthened and not become altogether sluggish. For God’s counsel cannot be mistaken; and since the divine Scriptures are writings according to the counsel of his will, it necessarily follows that they are true and in no way false. They were human beings by whom the divine Scriptures were handed down to us; they certainly wrote in words customary in human usage, with which they might signify to posterity what that supreme excellence of divinity willed to be known to mortals. Therefore you who now, devoted to secular wisdom, attack the divine Scriptures, say this: the Scripture of the New and Old Testament, which the Church of Christians has received and venerates as true, authentic, and holy, from where do you believe it was received? From God, or from human beings? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks Scripture while believing it to be inspired by God most plainly resists the divine ordinance. But if it is from human beings, why do you hope in it for the eternal salvation promised there, which a human being cannot give? Unless perhaps you madmen go on to say that all things are fabricated, and that after death nothing remains but ashes, and that the mind perishes together with the body; by that profession you would show yourselves no less insane than foolish. For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit. But if, made like apostates in a reprobate mind, you say that they were fabricated by human beings, then in your impious wandering in darkness you show how far you are from true wisdom.

You openly show that you are unskilled and rash judges, since you condemn Scripture which you do not understand. But because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it does not belong to this work to weary the mind any longer against the rashness of the unskilled. This one thing I want you to know: no one understands unless he receives; but because you place the filth of your affections in the way, so that you may not receive, therefore you do not have the understanding of true wisdom. For almighty God, the illuminator, deigns to be present by grace to those who, stripped of carnal desires, burn with the fire of inward love, who desire nothing in this world except God. The Spirit of God brings the aid of his presence to those whom he finds rooted in the love of truth, and, when they have been cleansed of every foreign thing, introduces them into knowledge of all things. For to those who truly love God all things are open, all things bare, all things manifest, since whoever through love beholds all things in faith in Jesus Christ, who creates and governs all things, knows everything necessary for his salvation. But on the contrary, from the slothful, the wicked, gluttons, the envious, the wrathful, the lustful, the filthy ...the filthy, the luxurious, murderers, impious and proud men, and those alien to piety, the illumination of God dwells very far away, permitting them to the judgment of the avenging demon, who, striking in the sharpness of savage fire, afflicts their senses and mind, and all the more arms and drives the impious to commit crimes, so that, guilty of a more shameful fault, they may also become liable to a harsher punishment. Hence, entangled in vices and worldly desires, they not only cannot penetrate the divine Scriptures by understanding, but even, neglecting themselves, they do not know themselves.

Since, therefore, sacred Scripture is the perfect work of God, Caesar, we ought so to confirm our mind that we believe it true, right, whole, solid, divinely inspired, and most abundantly sufficient for all who understand it for the confirmation of the Christian faith. Indeed, unless divine Scripture is believed to be true, holy, perfect, and whole in all things, the Christian faith would be deprived of its foundation. Therefore every Christian must take the greatest care that, by examining the divine Scriptures more than is expedient, he not pass beyond the bounds of piety, because man is not the author of the Scriptures, but the Holy Spirit; and whoever struggles against the integrity of God’s Scriptures is convicted of resisting his ordinance.

Moreover, Scripture, by God’s ordering, is usefully interwoven with parables, enigmas, similitudes, and comparisons of figures, so that those who read may be exercised toward understanding, and the mind, having tasted its inward sweetness, may be strengthened toward piety. Therefore, if with purified minds we attend to the sense of the Scriptures and not to the words, we shall understand how rightly and properly all things have been ordered. For it was not fitting that the sacred Scriptures, in which knowledge of the divine majesty is handed down, should be so plain and manifest that they might everywhere be understood by all, since it is set before good and holy persons alone to be understood, not also before evil, filthy, and polluted minds.

Hence it is written: “The beast that touches the mountain shall be overwhelmed with stones.” What is designated here by the beast, except human beings living like brute animals, without the love of God, in the pleasures of the flesh? And what is expressed by the mountain, except the height of the divine Scriptures? When the beast approaches this holy mountain, it is overwhelmed with stones, because a person impure in mind and weak in faith, who strives to search out the height of the divine Scriptures without a teacher handing it down, is wounded by various and destructive errors, as if by blows of stones. For just as all things are clean to the clean, so all things seem profane to the profane. God has therefore made the height of the Scriptures his hiding place; it is so inaccessible and closed to the reprobate that nevertheless it always lies open and manifest to the saints.

But why almighty God did not give holy Scripture as sufficient and manifest for all things that concern the Christian faith, we answer briefly. There are two things which the Most High provided for believers for the confirmation of the Christian faith: namely, the Church and Scripture, so that what is not expressed clearly enough in one may be more fully declared by the other. Hence, if we find anything about the rules of faith expressed less sufficiently in the holy Scriptures, we immediately have recourse to the Church; and where the Church has need of saving instruction for piety, at once it betakes itself to Scripture. From this it follows that neither would have it without Scripture, so that from the two one judgment may be made. For Augustine says: “I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church compelled me.” Ioannes John Gerson says: “I would not believe the Church unless the Gospel compelled me.” The Church confirms holy Scripture, and she herself is confirmed in like manner by Scripture. The Church abounds whenever Scripture is lacking, and if at any time the Church is in doubt, she has recourse to the counsel of Scripture. For there is one Holy Spirit of God who founded the Church in the faith of Jesus Christ, the same almighty Spirit who alone inspired Scripture. And this is the threefold cord that is not easily broken, where divine Scripture is joined through the Holy Spirit to the authority of the Church, to such a degree that the Church commends Scripture, and Scripture in turn commends the Church.

Therefore, as it seems to me, O Caesar of unconquered majesty, we have assigned a sufficient cause for the proposed question: because if everything that concerns the piety of faith were plainly expressed in the holy Scriptures, holy mother Church would not seem to have such great authority, and the merit of saving obedience would in large part be emptied away. At the same time, I think enough has been answered to the principal question, where some suppose that sacred Scripture is confused and imperfect in very many places; yet if they read it with due purity of mind, they would certainly find it perfect and solid. Great is the authority of the Catholic Church, which alone, in doubtful matters concerning faith, has the right to interpret the Scriptures; to her the necks of all powers must be subjected, and if anyone with rash daring departs from her definition, he has denied the Gospel of Christ. There is one congregation of the faithful, the mother of Christians, the holy Church; outside her unity no one will be saved. And although she may sometimes seem weak in morals, nevertheless, always constant in faith, she has never erred, by Christ’s mercy.

On the Reprobate and Maleficent Women. Question Five.

Question Fifth

The fifth question of your most serene highness was this: Why can impious, evil, and reprobate people in matters of faith, such as those women whom we commonly call maleficent women, command malign spirits, when good men and the most devoted observers of the Christian faith can command neither good spirits nor always malign ones?

I remember that I formerly answered this question as follows. In all the works of the divine majesty there is a sequence and order of beauty, of inviolable equity, by which individual things, suitably arranged, persevere in the rank they have received. For without its proper order, the freedom of choice that the Creator of all gave to human beings is driven by no violence of power, so that it does not always remain in the order that the first man received from the beginning of his creation. Hence no one among mortals is good except by the counsel of his own will, assisted through the grace of the merciful God; and no one is evil except by his own accord, deprived of grace because of the obstacle of sin.

By uprightness of will, however, we are made like the good spirits, if we prove the piety of the faith that we have in Christ by holy and necessary works. And just as the consummation of a good will makes good human beings equal to angelic spirits, so the perversity of the impious renders them like demons. Hence, the more evil and perverse people have been depraved by the malice of their own will, the more they become like demons in affection. By likeness, however, friendship and familiarity are introduced, from which mutual confidence is gradually generated. From the confidence of the lesser toward the greater, authority arises, whether it is true authority or one feigned by cunning. Therefore, if wicked people appear to have any command over demons, it arises from the magnitude of their depravity: namely, when their affection is depraved to such a degree that, by a reprobate will, they either surpass or equal the malice of the demons who join themselves to them.

For demons are not all equal in malice or intelligence, but one is much more cunning than another in agility of understanding, and far worse in depraved affection. For those who, falling from their high seats, are more closely joined to the earth and inhabit caverns and caves are certainly duller than the rest, to such a degree that they fear even swords and rods and seem to be warned by the threats of terrifying human beings, just as one may observe in those whom we call demoniacs. But the demons who dwell farther removed from the earth are of a subtler nature and more rarely meet with human beings. Human beings full of malice, however, the more they advance in perversity of will, the more like they become to demons, by whom, once admitted into familiarity, they thereafter become bold. once admitted into familiarity, thereafter become bold and receive command over the demons whose familiarity they enjoy, not by the violence of power but by feigned simulation. For demons, in order to keep as willing participants in their wickedness those men whom they have once received into surrender, gladly subject themselves to them under a simulated dominion, and what they do of their own accord they pretend to do as though compelled to obedience. For no one obtains true command over demons except one whom faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merit of holiness, has made acceptable and a friend to God. For thus Scripture says of those who truly believe in the Lord Jesus: “And he gave them power over all demons.”

Therefore evil men command demons because malice has made them like them, likeness familiar with them, and familiarity their own and subject to them. It is as if some servant of low birth, joined by long familiarity to a great prince, as often happens, were said to command him, since he obtains from him without contradiction everything he has asked, so that he seems rather to rule his lord than to be ruled by him. According to this likeness, evil and reprobate men who are admitted by demons into familiarity with them, and who become very bold through prolonged confidence, receive a simulated, not to say familiar, command over them, which they have deserved by the likeness of their most depraved will. Hence whatever they have demanded from demons who cooperate with them by an implicit or explicit compact, they receive, except whenever, being forbidden by divine ordinance, the demons cannot provide what is requested. Yet they do not cooperate in this way indiscriminately with all the reprobate and wicked, but only with those with whom, through the intervention of some compact, they have entered into covenants, such as evil-working women who have rendered homage to the devil, and those invokers of demons whom the common people call by the usual name necromancers.

There are two kinds of people who may lawfully command demons.

The first is that of those people who, beloved by God through the merit of holiness, have received from him the power of crushing the head of the ancient serpent. Such in the primitive Church were the apostles and their followers and disciples, of whom the Lord speaks in the holy Gospel: “In my name they will cast out demons, and they will take up serpents.”

The second kind is that of those people to whom, by reason of order in the Church of God, it is granted that by the power of the ministry they have received they may drive demons from human bodies. And this ministry is entrusted to exorcists in the Church of God when they are ordained by the pontiff.

Again, there are two kinds of people who desire to command demons, and their most wicked conditions show how unlawfully they presume to do so.

The first and most pernicious kind is that of witches, who enter into pacts with demons and, after a solemn profession has first been made, hand themselves over to some demon’s right of ownership and perpetual service. How great the evils are that this most pernicious kind of people commits in your empire, most wise Caesar, no one can express. For first of all, denying God, the faith of Christ, and holy baptism, they offer themselves in mind and body to demons; by their maleficent arts they sicken, harm, and kill human beings and beasts. There is no disease which, with God permitting, they cannot bring about, because, when they present themselves to demons as servants in observance of the compacted covenant, by comparison with them they dare whatever they wish.

Hence they are nowhere to be tolerated, but rather must be utterly exterminated in every place, as God, the creator of all things, commands: “You shall not permit sorcerers to live.” Some witches summon demons by charms; others entice them by prayers and sacrifices; the rest, provoking them with unspeakable things and ceremonies, draw them into the aid of their impiety. It is therefore no wonder that witches seem to command demons, since through the impiety of a perverse will they have become like them, and by mutual association they are united for the harm of the human race.

The second kind of depraved people wishing to command demons is that of those whom the common people call necromancers. They profess arts full of curses, by which they promise that they can call demons into a circle, or show them openly visible, enclosed in a crystal or some other vessel. These pernicious people, full of falsehood and superstitions, commit evils so great that no good person could imagine them. For in order to entice demons into their service, they very often use filthy sacrifices and enter into an express pact with them. They carry around many and various little books, full of foul impiety and falsehood.

...full of the filthiest impiety and lies, falsely inscribed with the names of ancient philosophers and sages. By displaying these they deceive many of the unwary and curious, and draw them with themselves into the pit of demons. They promise great and utterly incredible things; when men hear them, they falsely hold them suspended in wonder. By rings, pentacles, images, exorcisms, and conjurations, they say that they can constrain malignant demons so that they appear visibly in a circle, or in crystal, or in some other receptacle, and answer distinctly all questions put to them. All indeed promise this, but in our times very few are found whom malignant spirits obey, even in this way, since God, for a most just reason, does not permit it, lest the curiosity of men, prone to novelties, having despised the religion of Christ, should in time of need seek help from demons. But all those whom malignant spirits obey when summoned by the conjurations of necromancers have without doubt passed into fellowship with them by an explicit or implicit pact. As for the rest, their number is greater: malignant spirits disdain to obey them, although at all times they do not fear to occupy themselves in the profane arts of necromancers.

And because in our times especially iniquity has begun to abound and the charity of many has grown cold, these accursed and most mendacious men have become exceedingly strong; and although they are despised by demons, nevertheless, persisting in their pernicious doctrines, they deceive many. Believe me, Caesar, this most mendacious class of men is very harmful to your sacred empire, and therefore must be utterly exterminated no less than the brood of witches. They promise great things, and everything they say is a lie. Indeed, all the things promised in their books are vain and false, and provide believers with nothing but tricks, frauds, and the most subtle deceptions. But if at any time they seem to produce what they have promised, it should be clear to everyone that this happens only by the cooperation of demons; and fellowship with them must be fled no less than the most savage torments of hell. For demons very often come to these necromantic operations, and, in order to keep their invokers obstinate in the treachery they have begun, if they can, they grant them what they ask. Sometimes, however, when invoked by conjurations, they disdain to appear, and nevertheless have led astray the minds of those invoking them.

There is also another kind of men, no less foolish than superstitious, namely those who wish to have no commerce with demons, and nevertheless in their vain operations use things appropriated to demons, and for that reason utterly illicit. For they think that a great and hidden power inheres in characters, and therefore they commit various errors against the faith of Christ. But since it is not the business of this occasion to recount their madness, let us pursue our proposed subject.

Why good and just men do not obtain command over demons must be stated briefly. Just as likeness of wills makes evil and impious men equal to demons, so unlikeness of wills makes good and just men altogether contrary to them. But between contraries and those unlike one another there can be no familiarity; rather, continual opposition and hatred prevail. Where, however, there is no familiarity contracted by likeness of wills, there can be neither confidence of one toward another nor mutual cooperation in the performance of wonders. Nor do you, glorious Caesar, since you are a man and a great ruler and prince of men, admit as familiar to you anyone whose morals are altogether contrary and unlike your own...

41 unlike you, and continually resisting your will. But good and upright men, because they always resist the utterly depraved will of demons, can by no means pass into fellowship with those with whom they neither wish nor consent to be familiar; rather, with all their strength they flee and detest their approach. And therefore they do not obtain that feigned dominion over them of which I have spoken. For there is never any safe familiarity where no likeness of wills has preceded it; nor can there be concord between opposites, nor is friendship established between those unlike in will. Yet demons do not obey all evil and reprobate men indiscriminately, but only those with whom they are allied by pacts and services; and when invoked, they willingly come to those whom they cannot otherwise keep faithful, although they lie that they are compelled. It is therefore no wonder, excellent Caesar, that malignant spirits sometimes seem to obey wicked and perverse men, whom, as we have said, both malevolence like their own and destructive hostility toward the human race have made concordant. But let it be far from every Christian to wish to rule demons by a wicked likeness of will, because if anyone in this life begins to have fellowship with malignant spirits, in the future he will burn with them without end. But why can good and just men not command the holy angels of God, into whose likeness they have passed by goodness of will? I think that, from what has been said, a solution to this question would easily be given, if the difference among intellects is recalled. For although there are many men established in the church of God whose justice benefits many unto salvation, nevertheless in our times very few advance so far that, by the merit of sanctity, they are either feared by demons or received by angels into the fellowship of familiarity. Hence it happens that the men of our age neither command malignant spirits by merit of sanctity nor deserve to be familiar with the holy angels. But if any have advanced to that degree of sanctity by which, performing miracles in the church, the saints once advanced, then they can both command demons with power and have the familiar fellowship of blessed spirits. For it is certain that holy men beloved by God in the primitive church of Christians once bestowed greater benefits upon mortals through the operation of good spirits 42 than the impiety of wicked men could ever have inflicted through the ministry of demons in malefices. For anyone who is a true worshiper of God, if he has become like the holy angels, can do many marvelous things by prayers.

Question Six — On the Power of Witches

The sixth question of your invincible majesty was: Whence comes this power, so great in witches, by which they can perpetrate so many varied and marvelous things, even in a single hour, such as no one of the good could do, either in kind or in number, in his whole life?

If we wish to answer this question briefly, we must necessarily say that every power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything. For Christ says in the holy Gospel: Without me you can do nothing. Hence it is manifest that every power of doing anything is granted to human beings by the Lord God and from no other source, whether people do good or evil. Therefore the most holy bishop Augustine says: The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions, and nothing happens in this whole commonwealth of creation so very wide and immeasurable, visibly, unless it is either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments. Hence, Caesar, it must not be doubted that that power of witches, by which, with the cooperation of demons, they produce marvelous and horrible effects, is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist, and without whose influence a human being cannot even move his hand. For the holy doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything, whether to harm a person or a beast, unless almighty God wills it, consents to it, and grants the power for them to do what they have already decreed by a perverse will. Unless God consents and wills it, no creature can do anything. Otherwise, if something could happen when he did not will and consent to it, it would necessarily follow that God was weak, since he could not prohibit what he would be forced, against his will, to permit to happen. But because every human being, insofar as he is a creature, depends on God, he can do nothing without the will of him from whom he has both willing and power. Whatever, therefore, witches do is done by God's permission, ...without whose will they can do nothing; for unless God granted that they could do what they wish, they would obtain it neither from themselves nor from demons. Thus every power is from the Lord God, in whom all things both exist and are moved, as in the first cause of all things, since from him from whom we receive freedom of will, from him also we have the ability to do what we will.

But since the understanding of witches is very confused, they do not perpetrate the evils they do by human art, but by the cooperation of demons, whom both their subtle nature and long experience have made swift in producing marvels. For the astonishing effects of witches are not caused by such means as they use for witchcraft, such as heads of the dead, toads, serpents, characters, images, and things like these, but by the devil who instituted these signs; since he is most proud, he desires in all things to seem comparable to God. For indeed, just as almighty God instituted certain sacraments in his Church, which, when worthily administered and with himself assisting, signify and produce a salutary effect, with him who instituted them working salvation, so also the devil, who desires nothing more than to be esteemed equal to God, instituted certain signs as though they were sacraments. When invoked by those with whom he has been joined by pacts, that malignant operator assists them, and as often as God permits, he carries out the evil for which he is asked; if God does not permit it, he does absolutely nothing. Indeed, the devil is the operator of all necromantic and witchcraft effects; by applying the means that he himself had previously instituted to the subject matter, he produces the desired work, sometimes in reality, sometimes only in appearance.

Women who are witches, after passing by depraved will and consent through pacts into fellowship with demons, receive certain marks and symbolic signs from them; when these are used to summon them, the demons soon come. In these pernicious operations of demons, nothing is stronger than the foolish credulity of witches, which is increased by pacts and marks, since the firmer the faith they place either in demons or in their signs, the more swiftly they obtain the operation through their cooperation. For the exceedingly savage depravity of the witches’ will turns them in a certain way into frenzy; when this frenzy has taken possession of their mind, the demons soon attach themselves to the raging women, and, with God permitting, they grant to the frenzied women the effect of their petition, fortified by pacts and signs.

For Plato related something similar in the book On Poetic Frenzy, saying: just as Bacchant women, when not of sound mind, draw honey and milk from rivers, but when of sound mind cannot draw them. Their spirit, carried outside itself into fellowship with an evil demon, brings this about. We have found that witches in disturbed rivers have drawn butter at appointed times, which can in no way happen except by the ministry of a demon.

In the same way, when they have been brought into hatred of some man or beast and long for its death, they are driven by a most grievous frenzy, thinking in their soul of nothing except vengeance. They take up things known and familiar to them for witchcraft, invoke demons, display the signs instituted by them and also the characters, and what they cannot accomplish by their own power they obtain by the ministry of those demons. But another person, who is not subjected and devoted to demons by pact, even if he knows the things suitable for witchcraft and also the manner of operation, and although he displays the signs, nevertheless rarely obtains the effect, because he is not counted among the familiars of the demons. For the devil, swollen with pride, imitates the Church of Christ to such a degree that... just as one who has not been ordained cannot consecrate the body of Christ, however much he utters the words of consecration, so too a demon, however much someone invokes him and displays signs and characters, either never or only rarely comes to the aid of one whom he does not know to be subject to him by pact. For if he came indiscriminately to all who invoked him, without pacts having been made, he would not possess so many witches dedicated to him by right of ownership.

Hence it is that many people devoted to profane arts, laboring with dreadful conjurations to summon demons to a circle, a mirror, or any other receptacles, obtain no effect, because either God’s command stands in the way, or the devil despises the curious person who has not been dedicated to him by homage.

For three things are required for witchcraft, without which it is agreed that none is perpetrated: a witch frenzied in mind and depraved in will, the cooperation also of a familiar devil, and before all else divine permission. For if one of these does not concur, witchcraft cannot be perpetrated. For if God did not permit it, neither the devil nor the witch could do anything. And if the devil did not come to meet the will of the depraved woman, she would perpetrate no witchcraft.

Again, if the witch were lacking, the devil would in no way complete the witchcraft. For the devil uses the will of the frenzied witch as an artisan uses an instrument for working; without it he could not inflict witchcraft. And just as demons differ from one another in power and in keenness of subtlety, so the power of witches is not the same in all of them, but differs in individuals according as demons of subtler or grosser nature join with them.

For there are many kinds of demons, and they stand apart from one another in definite ranks, according to the places into which they were thrust down when they fell in the beginning. The first kind of demons is called fiery; it ranges about the upper air and is never cast down to lower regions before the day of judgment, but, remaining continually beneath the lunar regions, has no intercourse with human beings on earth. That they remain beneath the moon is attested by Saint Augustine in the work On the Christian Combat, speaking thus: Demons do not dwell in heaven, where the sun and stars are, but all move about beneath the lunar region.

Moved by this, as I think, Apuleius said that demons are fiery animals, because Aristotle confirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals have often been seen flying about, fitted with little wings, which spend their whole lifetime in fire, since they are born with fire and are extinguished with it, and, vanishing, return to their own place from which they had come. They have no association with witchcraft, because, since they dwell in fire, on account of their subtlety they cannot put on a gross or airy body.

The second kind is called airy, which wanders in the air and dwells near us. These can descend to lower places and, after assuming bodies from the thicker air, sometimes appear visibly to human beings. When God permits it, they often trouble the air, stir up thunder and storms, and all conspire together for the destruction of the human race. They are moved by passions of feeling in the manner of human beings, especially by pride and envy; they are touched by continual disturbances, and they are neither clothed in a solid body nor remain in one place. Nor do they all have one form, but many, and these they change rather often, according to the variety of the feelings by which they either come when summoned by the spells of little witches, or are driven by disturbance to do harm. For they have 46 For they have an altogether violent and furious disposition, full of disturbances; hence, when they have been violently harmed and disturbed, they very suddenly devise many snares, and while they carry out their assaults, in part they wish to remain hidden, and in part they inflict violence. Witches, supported by the cooperation of these demons, are more powerful for working witchcraft in proportion as they have obtained the cooperation of one higher in their order. In the Life of Saint Anthony, Saint Athanasius said that the air is full of demons, which Mercury Trismegistus had said before him: namely, that no part of the world is deprived of the presence of demons. The holy bishop Ambrose also says: “The world is full of holy powers, because it is full of wickedness.” Hence the Platonists have handed down that demons flying in the air like very dense fiery snow become visible to those who wish it, if for some time, while the sun is shining, they keep their gaze fixed toward heaven with unblinking eyes. But I do not know whether an object is produced in the air from a real consistency, or whether the restrained motion of the eyes presents false images; nevertheless, not without some slight harm to the sense, I have tested what was promised.

The third kind, however, we call terrestrial demons, whom we do not at all doubt to have fallen from heaven to earth according to their deserts. Concerning these, the most holy bishop and martyr of Christ, the God-bearer Ignatius, once wrote in a certain letter to the Ephesians as follows: “Nothing is better than to have peace, in which every weapon of the spirits of the air and of the earth alike is made void.” Of these demons, some dwell in forests and groves and lay snares for hunters; others live in open fields and make travelers wander by night; some dwell in hidden places and caves; the rest, less furious and disturbed than the others, delight in dwelling obscurely with human beings. They are not led by one affection but by various ones, since some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Of these, some rejoice in frightening human beings by illusions alone; others desire to draw those who hear them into admiration of themselves by predictions of future things. Some, however, strive with the greatest effort to terrify, injure, or kill human beings disturbed by irrational frenzy or raging with melancholy, which we know by experience has often happened. Hence Saint John 47 John Chrysostom, in the third book On Providence to the monk Stagirius, says: “The magnitude of grief is more powerful for doing harm than every diabolical action, because whomever the demon overcomes, he overcomes through grief. If you remove it, no one will be able to be harmed by the demon.” This kind of demon, however, is rarely familiar with witches, because of the inconstancy of its affections and the fickleness by which they rejoice in frightening many rather than submitting to the rule of one little woman. Yet sometimes, as they promise to frenzied women, they dwell in glass or in crystal or in a mirror, and, when stirred up by spells, give answers to women; and if anyone coming should have spoken ill of them, they foretell it on the way. And this kind of witches sometimes differs greatly from the rest, because what those other women make sick by witchcraft, these promise to cure. But because they for the most part repel witchcraft by witchcraft, access to them is forbidden by the Church to every Christian. The fourth kind of demon is called aquatic, because, immersing itself in waters, it dwells around lakes and rivers, full of anger, disturbed, restless, and deceitful; it stirs up storms at sea and, sinking ships into the deep, takes away the lives of many in the waters. And whenever these demons assume a visible body, they more frequently appear in the female sex, and are more rarely seen in the male, because they dwell in moist places and follow a softer course of life, nor can they easily assume a vile shape through association with the others. Hence antiquity long ago named the naiads and nereids, nymphs of the waters, not with the male sex but the female. Among our people, however, they are commonly called aquatic women, that is, wasserfrauwen. But those who dwell in drier and somewhat arid places, whenever they appear visibly to human beings in bodily form, transform themselves into men. They also assume the appearances of various beasts, according as they are touched by various affections. But the holy angels, because they are never varied in affection, always appear uniformly in male form. For nowhere do we read it written that a good spirit was seen in the form of a woman or of any beast, but always in the appearance of a man. Yet demons have often been seen around rivers and springs in the appearance of women, sometimes dancing in a ring, sometimes letting down their hair in the manner of women, and sometimes with human beings 43 speaking with human beings and practicing various mockeries. And this kind of demons is not accustomed to have commerce with witches. The fifth kind is called subterranean, because it dwells in caves and caverns and in the remote hollows of mountains. These demons are very wicked in disposition, and they especially attack those who dig wells and mines, and those who seek treasures hidden in the earth, being most ready for the destruction of the human race. They make openings in the earth, stir up flame-vomiting winds, and shake the foundations of buildings. Sometimes at night they go out from the mountains in troops and lead marvelous and astonishing dances in the fields; and, as though fearing the command of one leader, they suddenly vanish at a signal and return to their hiding places. Sometimes the sound of bells is heard among them, and they sometimes falsely claim to be the spirits of people who have died. They seek nothing more than the fear and amazement of human beings. Hence we have found that they have sometimes led certain simpler people into their hiding places in the mountains, showing astonishing spectacles to those who marveled, and falsely claiming to be friends of the living, as though the dwellings of the blessed were there. Among these demons also some are guardians of treasures, which the greed of mortals has hidden in the earth; and, lest they again come into human use, they carry them off, steal them, guard them, and sometimes move them from place to place. And this kind of demons is accustomed to have no commerce with witches.

The sixth kind of demons is called light-fleeing, because they especially dread and detest light: for they never appear by day, nor can they assume a body in any other way than by night. This is the business that walks about in darkness, a kind of demons unsearchable and utterly dark, driven by cold passions, malicious, restless, and disturbed. It violently assaults people it meets in the hours of night, and often, God permitting, kills some either by its breath or by its touch. This kind of demons does not associate with witches, nor can it be constrained by charms, because it flees light, human voices, and likewise every disturbance. The aerial kind especially is accustomed to come together for works of witchcraft and for women, because it is subtler than all the others and of the most reckless boldness. Of the terrestrial 49 kind also, as has been said, some serve witches; yet, since they are held to be of a lower rank, they are by no means able to bring about those greater works of witchcraft. It is therefore plainly evident that the whole power of witches, by which they do such marvelous things, is granted to demons in a limited way by the Lord God; and when he does not permit it, they accomplish nothing.

ON DIVINE PERMISSION. Seventh Question.

Question Seventh

The seventh question of your most serene Majesty was this: Why does God, since he is just and the avenger of evils, permit such great works of witchcraft to be done for the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners, but also many innocent people, perish after being grievously tormented?

I remember that, when I was formerly placed before your Majesty, I answered this question in this way. The best God, just and upright, devoted and merciful, whatever he permits, permits justly, because he is just and there is no injustice with him; rather, in true judgment he either does or permits all things that happen. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evils to happen, we answer: he permits them precisely because he is just. Let it not seem to your Majesty, O Caesar, that the answer we have given is absurd, since it in no way prejudices the divine goodness that he permits evils to happen for a most just reason; rather, it would prejudice it if he did not permit evils to happen in the present mode. For indeed, if he did not permit evils to happen, then a human being could not sin; he would certainly be incapable of sin, which does not suit his nature, to which the Creator of all things gave free will from the beginning. For a human being, since he is a creature and not the Creator, is necessarily able to turn both to good and to evil; his being depends on the supreme maker of all creatures, just as every caused thing depends on the cause of its own being. Creation itself has been left to God alone, who is incorruptible and everlasting; but every corruptible thing necessarily fails, and is preserved by the goodness of the Creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. Hence it neither could have happened, nor would it have been fitting, that a human being should be created by the condition of his nature incapable of sin; this is something in which only God, the maker of all things, naturally rejoices, who is unchangeable and everlasting. But whenever it is granted to a human being that he seems unable to sin, the freedom of choice is not removed, nor is possibility simply taken away, but the will is confirmed in good. And whenever this gift is conferred on a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature. For Scripture says: God created man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel. For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, should both have free choice and be unable to commit sin. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: The first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the last, in glory, will be much greater: to be unable to sin. And so, if man could not sin, he would not have mastery over his own will. Therefore, although almighty God does not will sin, he nevertheless justly permits human beings to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of choice remains, both the virtue of a good work may receive its reward, and voluntary wickedness may receive what evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly. Therefore almighty God justly permits human beings to sin and to do evil, since from the beginning he granted them freedom of choice. But there are many reasons long since assigned by the holy doctors why the Almighty permits such great acts of sorcery to be done through the cooperation of demons; we shall necessarily mention them briefly in order.

The first is so that the excellence of divine power may be made manifest, for he alone is unchangeable and far above every position. Every creature, however, is changeable and has no comparison with the unchangeable Creator. Hence it is read in Numbers: God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. In Isaiah also it is said: God is faithful, without iniquity, just and upright. In the book of Tobit too it is written: You are just, Lord, and all your judgments are true, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And in the book of holy Job we read: Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will repay a man’s work to him, and according to the ways of each he will restore to him. Therefore every man who rightly understands his own ignorance and weakness plainly recognizes what a nothing he is compared with his Creator. For God justly permits man to sin, both so that freedom of choice may continue and so that the excellence of the great God may become known to human beings.

The second reason is so that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, which knows how to draw good from our evils, since it makes one person’s sin become another’s merit for the increase of virtue. For if he did not permit evil to be done, which of us would understand the good? For God makes and orders the good; but evils he does not make, though when they have been done by the wicked, he disposes them so that they do not come about without order. Nor does the malice of human beings impede God’s will, nor can a human being do anything that God does not permit.

The third cause, moreover, is that the Almighty permits acts of sorcery to be done in order to manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and have done penance; he could in no way show this if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, God could not be merciful. But because we all offend in many things, everywhere God finds something to forgive; everywhere a guilty person presents himself, in whom the loving Creator may show his mercy. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: If the illness were slight, the physician would be disregarded; he would not be sought. If the physician were not sought, the illness would not be ended. Therefore, where sin abounded, grace also abounded, which alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, heaps together into one. Therefore the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason for divine permission is so that the justice of the Creator may be declared against those who have sinned and have not done penance; for if all did good and no one sinned, God’s justice would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have its place, by divine permission the creature sins. For the Lord is just, and he will render to each according to the works of his will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition, because if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem lower than brute animals, which, with no violence driving them, freely use the motions of nature. For although brute animals lack reason, they nevertheless have a free motion of nature, which they follow. In comparison with them, man would seem to be of a lower condition if he did not have the will of free choice. But God permitted man a free will, over which neither kings nor princes rule.

The sixth reason is the praise of the merit of human constancy 52 of virtue, when we praise a just man for this reason, that although he could have transgressed, he did not transgress, but, with the grace of God helping him, remained steadfast in a good will.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits demons to do such great evils through the agency of witches is that those who, having despised the truth, delight in falsehood may be utterly deceived, seduced by the devil, the inventor of falsehood. For it is fitting that enchanters and witches, who disdain to follow the saving teachings of Christ, should all, deceived by demons, be plunged down to hell to be punished forever. They seek help from demons, the enemies of the whole human race, and they despise the Savior of the world, whom alone they ought to have adored. For it is just that one who deserts the truth by his own voluntary will and clings to falsehood should be hurled by the devil into destruction.

The eighth cause is the manifestation of divine power, whose might and strength are over every creature. Indeed, when almighty God sometimes permits great things to the devil and denies him certain small things, he shows how weak the enemy of the human race is, and how subject in all things to the divine majesty. For the devil can do nothing of himself,

G 4. but all that he does, he does with God permitting it. Therefore the first cause of all, on account of which almighty God permits evils to be done, is justice, by which he preserves in an inviolable order the freedom which he once bestowed on the creature from the beginning. But because every power of a creature dependent on its Creator is restricted and limited, it is clear that neither the devil can do everything he wishes, nor man, however depraved in will. The will is indeed free, but power is limited by fixed and necessary degrees. For if demons could do everything they wish, nothing among human affairs would remain safe, but they would throw everything into ruin.

The history of holy Job shows by a clear example the bound power of demons, for Satan did not dare to tempt him beyond what had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. For no one in the present world, however just or strong, could resist the fury of demons if, at their own discretion, they could always use a free power of harming. Before the Lord’s Passion, however, they enjoyed greater freedom of power than afterward; but when Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, their power was already thereafter greatly 53 reduced. The Savior says in the Gospel: Now the prince of the world will be cast out. For the humility of Christ and the perseverance of the saints have greatly restrained the boldness of demons, so that they can rightly be called inciters of evils, but by no means drivers. Nor would the devil gain strength against us unless he received his strength from our sins. Hence Scripture admonishes us, saying: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. And again: Do not give place to the devil.

Therefore, in concluding this discourse for the understanding of the proposed question, why God permits so many evils to be done, I believe the reasons have been sufficiently made clear. For even if the will of demons is always wicked, their power can never be unjust, because what he wickedly wills he has from his own choice, but what he is able wickedly to do he has only from God.

And these things have been said insofar as they concern those who do evil. But why does almighty God permit demons to harm, through the agency of witches, people who have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity and faithfully believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? For if they could harm only the wicked, the perverse, and unbelievers in body and goods, but were restrained from access to and injury of the good and faithful, the just judgment of this permission would rightly seem clear. But now, more often, the good and innocent are made sick by the evils of demons, and sometimes they are even deprived of life, to pass over in silence the loss of temporal goods which those bewitched often suffer; and it becomes a matter of doubt for many why the Almighty permits these things, since he permits nothing unjustly.

For this proposed question I shall set out, as briefly as I can and in order, the necessary reasons which I have received from none other than the ancient and catholic doctors. The first reason is the testing of Christians’ faith and the proving of their integrity, so that, scourged by the evils of demons, they may learn in the sufferings of the flesh what faith and love toward God they have hidden in the mind. To be long-suffering in prosperity is not difficult; but in adversities, with humble patience, to await help from the Savior of the faithful belongs not to the soft, but to the strong and truly faithful Christians. In his tribulation most holy Job learned how great a constancy of faith he had toward God, though before, in tranquility, in tranquillity had preserved piety without the dart of temptation. Hence it must also be noted that those whom works of witchcraft by demons or by human beings have in any way made ill, and who, in order to recover health, either approach or consult any witches and enchanters, whether by themselves or through others, act against the commandments of God and of the Church, and have neither true faith in God nor love. For they prefer the health of their mortal flesh to God, and seek salvation not from Christ but from the devil and his minister. For they prefer to be healthy in the name of the devil and live unhappily, rather than to suffer a little here for the love of Christ and afterward rejoice with him forever. But whoever does not approach witches because God has forbidden it, preferring to live in poverty and sickness while observing God’s commandments rather than, against God, in riches and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly preserves the integrity of the Christian faith. Among Christians, most sacred Caesar, men corrupted in mind and reprobate concerning the faith must not be tolerated: those who cure the bewitched by works of witchcraft, who reveal thefts and adulteries by the ministry of demons, who foretell future things by inspection of stones or mirrors.

Do not listen, I beg you, to those who, ignorant of the divine laws, think that ministers of demons of this sort are useful to your rule, because they know how to dissolve works of witchcraft by witchcraft; for that destructive cure of bodies brings death to souls, and makes human beings withdraw from God, the creator of all things, and cling to impious apostate demons, with whom after death they will be damned forever.

The second reason why almighty God permits the innocent to be harmed by witchcraft is the increase of merits, so that, when their patience has been tested in tribulation, they may merit a worthier crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says, a man is unknown to himself as to what he can bear and what he cannot bear. Sometimes he fears that he cannot do what nevertheless he can do. When temptation approaches, as though some interrogator, a man is discovered by himself, who, previously hidden, did not know himself. The divine arch-apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others as to how thoughtless and weak he was; when it came, the weakness that had been hidden appeared. Therefore temptation is the greatest proof of a human being, as Sacred Scripture bears witness: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous people.” Patience is easy in prosperity, since no adversity strikes the mind. But “many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from them all the Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.”

The third reason for divine permission is the preservation of humility, so that the faithful and righteous person may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or righteousness. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: “They are not in the labor of men, and they will not be scourged with men. Therefore pride has held them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety; their iniquity has come forth as though from fatness.” It belongs to the mercy of God that he sometimes permits good and righteous people to be shaken by adversities, whom he knows cannot be humbled in prosperity. For tribulation has made many humble whom favorable circumstances would have made proud. Finally, the fearful imagination of works of witchcraft makes a good person fear his God and diligently invoke his help; fortified by that help against the assaults of demons, he can trust that he is safe. But no one who is proud and presumes upon his own strength can protect himself from the works of witchcraft of the demon. let him think himself safe, because the man whom the protection of God has abandoned, puffed up by pride, without doubt lies open to the sorceries of demons.

The fourth reason is so that there may be a distinction between good men and bad. For Scripture says of good men beloved by God, in the Acts of the Apostles, that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. And Saint Paul, lover of Christ, says in a certain epistle: All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. The most wise King Solomon also says in Proverbs: The Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and, like a father, takes pleasure in his son. It is a very glorious thing for a Christian to endure adversities patiently for the love of God, whether they are inflicted by evil men or by demons. For power is given to the devil and his ministers to harm good and righteous men, not for their destruction, as robbers think, but rather for the very great and certain consolation of the soul. For indeed, when a righteous man lives well, harms no one, offends no one, does injury to no one, loves, fears, and venerates his God with his whole heart, keeping his commandments with every care, and nevertheless is troubled by sorcerers, whether in body, or in possessions, or in both, that man is truly blessed, because, when he has been proved, he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him. Everyone who lives rightly in the unity of the faith of the Catholic Church of Christians, and patiently endures for the love of God the evils he receives in this world, has a certain sign that he perseveres in the grace of God and will be saved. Therefore we read that it is written thus of the evil and reprobate: Why do the impious live, lifted up and strengthened with riches? Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them; they spend their days in good things, and in a moment they go down to hell. For it is a manifest sign of damnation if here you live wickedly in sins and vices, opposed to God, and prosper in the goods of fortune and in bodily health.

The fifth reason why the Almighty permits good and righteous men to be troubled by the evil and reprobate is the complete purification of the mind. For, as Scripture says, there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin. But since God lets no sin pass unpunished, he ordains for righteous men, through mercy, temporal punishments for their offenses, but for the impious and reprobate, through justice, eternal punishments. Therefore, out of mercy, he changes eternal punishment for the penitent into temporal punishment, which they must necessarily suffer either in this world or after death in purgatory. But because the torments of purgatory are dreadful and very grave, merciful God is accustomed to purify the penitents whom he loves in this life in various ways, through the hardships of diverse tribulations in body and in possessions. For the sorceries of the impious benefit good and righteous men as a remedy, but bring damnation upon those who inflict them.

The sixth reason is so that a man bewitched through the assaults of demons may be recalled to repentance, and may set in his heart the necessary amendment of life. For Almighty God does not send punishment immediately when we sin, but waits for our amendment until a fixed time. But if we have neglected to do penance, the avenger of evils comes to us when we do not expect it; and we who, as sinners, scorned to recognize ourselves by repenting in tranquillity, will at last recognize ourselves, too late, in tribulation. Hence the holy Prophet speaks in the person of God, saying: If his children forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with blows; but I will not take my mercy away from them, nor will I violate my truth.

The seventh reason why Almighty God permits the sorceries of demons to prevail against the good and innocent is so that an excessively licentious occasion for sinning may be cut off from them. For there are many poor and infirm people, pleasing to God, good, devout, and humble, whom poverty and bodily sickness preserve in the love of God; if they were rich and raised high with honors, they would quickly flow away from the resolve of holiness into the depth of vices. It is not expedient for everyone’s salvation to have honors and riches together with health, nor does a longer life always make a man better. Therefore Almighty God, wishing to show his mercy toward those whom he has chosen, permits the good, righteous, and innocent to be subject to various calamities, sometimes through demons, sometimes through evil men, and sometimes by various other means. and means, he takes away from such people riches and honors, which he foreknew they would use badly, so that in poverty and abasement they may preserve the humility which, placed in wealth and exaltation, they would by no means have preserved. He also very often permits many great illnesses to befall them, when cheerful bodily health would have brought the greatest sickness upon the mind. Finally, he permits certain people to be driven to death by harmful magic, so that the freedom for sinning may be cut away from them, which they would have abused if they had been allowed to live longer. Hence Scripture says of the righteous man: “He was taken away lest malice should change his understanding, and lest deceit should deceive his soul.”

The eighth reason for divine permission is so that human beings may venerate the sacraments of the Church, which have great power against all the harmful works of malign spirits. For one who venerates with due honor the sacraments and rites of the Catholic Church is rarely harmed by the harmful works of demons. And by the confession of witches themselves we have often heard that hearing Masses and using things blessed by the Church greatly weaken the powers of demons. For they are not blessed in the Church of God in vain, but so that they may be signs of divine protection, showing demons defenses to be feared. Concerning children and infants, however, who, reborn in Christ, are sometimes killed by the harmful works of demons or of human beings, we do not doubt that divine providence permits this to happen for their salvation, since it knows how to order all things for the better for mortals. Yet it often happens that infants perish by harmful magic because of the sins of their parents.

On the Providence of God, Question Eight.

Question Eighth

Your Serenity’s eighth question was this: whether it can be proved by natural reason, as well as by the holy Scriptures, that God has care for human affairs and actions, and a certain and infallible providence over all things, both collectively and individually, that are done in the world.

I remember that I replied to this question as follows: The whole world, heaven and earth and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence, by whose will and command they were brought into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us prove this opinion first from the Scriptures, and afterward, as briefly as possible, by reasons. In the book of Judith we read: “All your ways are prepared, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the most wise king Solomon speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth to make your soul sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps the Lord, angered by your words, scatter all the works of your hands.”

The clearest testimonies of providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel, where our Savior says to the disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for an as, and one of them does not fall to the ground before God?” Great is this commendation of divine providence, which has care not only for human beings but also for tiny birds. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would not believe that he has care for great things? “Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” And a little later he adds, saying: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more you, O you of little faith?” Because almighty God created all things and brought them into being when they did not exist, he rules and governs all things so that they may not slip away and perish; and this could in no way happen if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is removed, it necessarily follows that the continuous order of the whole universe is thrown into confusion.

The providence of the Creator cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds, gives beasts their food, fills every living thing with blessing, and clothes the grass of the field, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful splendor, cannot forget the human being whom he created from the beginning in his own image. He cares for all things who governs all things, and he exercises providence not only over the human being but also over all beasts, in whose dominion all things have been placed; and there is no one who can resist his will in anything.

Let us now, therefore, consider this immense structure of the whole universe: how it always continues in its original arrangement and motion, in the most orderly fashion; and unless we are shamefully out of our minds, by the clearest reasoning we shall understand that the immutable divine providence preserves, directs, and governs these things. Then Next, let us contemplate all earthly things: how each and every one is born and proceeds in its natural disposition in the most orderly fashion. This cannot happen by chance; rather, they must be moved by the will of him by whose power they were made and created. Likewise, let us contemplate the earth, placed in the middle of the world like a point or center, around which the whole universe unfolds at equal distance. Nothing more beautiful, nothing more adorned, nothing, finally, more delightful could offer itself to the senses for contemplation. In this point of an immense mass, enclosed by that mass itself, we see all things wonderfully ordered, and that nothing can be left unordered; so that all things which sometimes seem to us somehow to drift, we may know for certain, within the order of the universe, not to lack their own particular order. For by the simple and utterly unchangeable command of God, the whole structure of the entire universe, assembled out of so many diverse and movable things, works together and is ruled in the most orderly way. We certainly see, in those things that often present themselves to our senses, that the greater the intelligence and power that arises over time in any governor, the less can anything disordered happen there by random chance. Therefore, since that highest intellect, the creator, preserver, and ruler of all things, almighty God, rules and governs the world by his unchangeable providence, holding all things under his command, surely no place anywhere is left for rash chance, which could impede the will of so great a majesty.

Therefore the whole universe, whatever exists anywhere or can exist, is contained under the command of the one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. Unexpected accidents happen to us because we are changeable and are changed almost daily, having no determinate knowledge of future things. But that best maker of all things, God, since he is altogether unchangeable, knows all things, beholds all things, and understands all things together and at once. His providence is not deceived; his will is never changed; his power is not broken; his ordering is not violated; his counsel is never intercepted, even if his sentence sometimes seems to be changed. Hence, if we pay careful attention, we shall plainly understand that the ends of things and of motions will show that all these lower things come to be, are preserved, are arranged, and are moved by divine providence, to whose command absolutely nothing is alien. For God himself, the ruler of all things, understands both all things and each single thing, not stretched out, as we are, among many things, but remaining in himself, one and indivisible. In looking upon himself as the exemplar of the whole universe and the cause of causes, and through the causes contemplating the cause of all things, he cares for and provides for all things by contemplating them, directing each one to its end and good by an everlasting order. Come now, most wise Caesar: in order that we may understand divine providence governing all things, let us use arguments as brief as we can for our purpose. And so, if God’s action is his own intelligence, as no wise person fails to admit, since it is at once most eminent and most inward, then insofar as he acts, he surely understands, and conversely. But he acts in individual things, not only in great things but also in the smallest; therefore he understands individual things. For the most abundant influence of the first being extends through all things that in any way exist, following in fixed orders; and the things that act after him are everywhere moved by his power and act by it.

Either, then, God understands or does nothing outside himself, which is false; or, by acting, he also understands all things and each single thing, which is true. For they would nowhere come to be unless they were first, to speak in our manner, understood by God himself, who makes them, just as things are not brought about by the sun if they are not looked upon by it. But because the Almighty understands all things and each single thing that he makes, there is no doubt that he disposes, rules, and orders all things that he has made. From him things have not only that they exist, but also that they are certain causes of other things. And so, if things have from God that they are causes, from him also they received the proper office of a cause: that is, to preserve, according to their powers, and to care for what they have made. Therefore, if all causes have this property from the first cause, insofar as they are certain causes, deservedly that first cause naturally has this goodness and providence, so that he cares for all things and each single thing that he has made, since he is most especially the cause of all and each of them. Indeed, unless individual things are guarded one by one by him who makes them, the common things that are preserved in individual things will never be guarded. For the whole that consists of parts will not be preserved if the parts themselves are neglected. are neglected. Therefore, from the intention of the first and greatest intelligence comes the common and universal distinction of things. It is distinguished from others by itself, and it distinguishes the rest among themselves by the standard of its own conception. Hence, just as God knows all things and each thing most distinctly, so too he most distinctly rules, governs, and cares for them.

I think, therefore, most clement Caesar Maximilian, that it is clear and sufficiently shown that the providence of God, the supreme ruler, embraces, disposes, rules, and governs all lower things and each one of them; otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who watches over them, they would by no means continue in this most beautiful order that we discern.

Nor does it escape me how variously the wise men of this world once held opinions about providence. Some of them thought that this world was made not by providence but by chance. If their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence; rather all things would necessarily drift, and the world, since it was made by chance, could perish by chance. Against their false opinion others taught that the world could not have been made without reason, nor certainly continue to exist, unless it were ruled by the highest providence of its maker. Hence Boethius, that most Christian man, said: “O you who govern the world by everlasting reason, sower of earth and heaven, who command time to go forth from eternity, and, remaining stable, grant that all things be moved.” And again he said: “The generation of all things, all the advances of changeable natures, and whatever is moved in any way, receive their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.”

Others, however, thought that God cared only for incorruptible things, such as the heavenly bodies and separate substances, and likewise the species of things, but that he was entirely ignorant of all the rest and utterly neglected them. But these men erred shamefully, because the Almighty has providence and care not only for universal and incorruptible things, but also for particular and corruptible things. Hence Saint Boethius again says: “The lofty founder of things sits upon the earth, and, ruling all things, bends the reins: king and lord, fountain and origin, law, and wise arbiter of justice. He is the continuous love for all things, and they seek to be held by the end of the good, because they cannot endure otherwise unless, turned back again by love, they flow back to the causes that he himself gave.”

Others, however, unable to bear that they should be neglected, removed man from the number of corruptible things because of the preeminence of his intellect, saying that God has care and providence for man, but despises all the remaining earthly things. Against their false opinion I think enough has already been said, and to bring forward many things would be wholly superfluous. For Scripture says: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord.” And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made the small and the great, and he has equal care for all.”

Therefore the providence of the divine majesty orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all lower things and each one of them, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible; his most powerful will produced all things from nothing, as sacred Scripture again bears witness: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.” Let men corrupt in mind, impious, and reprobate concerning the Christian faith therefore blush, who, puffed up by mere loquacity, take away the providence of him who knows all things, and do not consider how great an injury they do to God. For what, to use the judgment of Firmianus, is so worthy of almighty God, and so proper to him, as providence? But if he foresees nothing, if he neglects lower things, if he does not care for mortal things, he has now lost all dignity. But it is impossible, as Saint Anselm attests, for God to lose his honor, since, as the Peripatetic says, “in eternal things there is no evil, no corruption, and no sin.” Whoever, therefore, removes providence removes the whole substance of God; and what does he say except that God does not exist?

But now let those who deny that God’s providence cares for lower things tell me: if God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, then there is no longer any reason why we should pursue him with worship or venerate him with religion, since we obtain no benefit from him; rather, neglected and despised, we ourselves should neglect him too.

But if, not knowing, he despises and neglects us, then there is plainly no reason for us to worship him, since he does not know us and for that reason is unable to confer any good, or to call upon him in prayers. For if God does not care for human affairs, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every reason for piety ceases, since there is no hope of salvation. of salvation. What regard for piety can there be among mortals, what hope for the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence is removed, whom do we worship, whom do we adore? If there is no providence for mortals with God, certainly he neither bestows benefits on human beings, nor imposes punishments on deserters, nor can help mortals, nor wishes to, nor cares at all; nor does he notice what we do, and he hears neither the prayers nor the petitions of anyone. Why then do we offer him any worship, why honor, why prayers? Or why do we so greatly fear or dread a God who does not know us, who, having neglected and despised us, can do us neither good nor harm?

For when providence has been removed, neither holiness nor religion will remain; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and dreadful confusion will follow. With piety toward God removed, what will the commonwealth now be except everlasting confusion? Public trust among human beings will necessarily perish; and the society of the human race, and all justice together with it, will vanish and perish. What is to be thought of the Christian faith, if God does not care for human affairs? What, finally, is to be thought of the Savior of all the living, our Lord Jesus Christ, unless the whole thing will be reckoned an empty tale and a fiction, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? Therefore whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is wholly vain and useless to us, if he has no care for us at all.

Let those who deny the providence of God now see and tremble, when they behold the end of their opinion: the worst despair of all. Therefore let no one, led on by the empty talk of worldly philosophers, train himself in contempt of God; let no one remove the providence of the highest and unchangeable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of and ungrateful for the benefits of the most merciful Savior.

For it must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole universe, both visible and invisible, and all and each of the things that are either in heaven or on earth or in the sea, are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the whole universe is alien to his care. For divine providence provides for the human race crops and all the other things the earth brings forth, and also storms, the varieties of seasons, and the changes of the sky, by which all the things the earth produces ripen and grow mature. It cares for all and each, not only the great things but even the very smallest, so much so that not even the thinnest leaf of a tree falls to the ground without the will of almighty God the Father, who created it and rules and cares for it.

But if anyone thinks that this whole magnitude of the entire universe cannot be ruled and governed by the one God, who alone is God, he is greatly mistaken, and is shown not to know how great the power of divine might is. Indeed, he who was able to bring the whole world from nothing into being can also govern forever, with the greatest wisdom, what he has made. For he knows all things, understands all things, and can do all things, he alone, omnipotent, who created all things.

Therefore we, believing the holy Gospel, should above all venerate divine providence; and, with what virtue we can, we should raise our minds upward from these things that are perishable, and, brought back to ourselves, be united, so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God present everywhere. Since it is wholly uncircumscribable, it holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things.

But it does not sustain from one part and surpass from another, nor fill from one part and encompass from another; rather, by encompassing it fills, and by filling it encompasses; by sustaining it surpasses, and by surpassing it sustains all things. By the mass of a body he is nowhere, and by his uncircumscribable substance he is nowhere absent. He is not perceived by the eyes of flesh; he is seen through faith in purity of heart.

O inexpressible power. O incomprehensible goodness. O ineffable wisdom. O uncircumscribable divinity, which does not consist of parts, as a body does; is not endowed with passions, as a soul is; does not subsist in forms, as all other things do that have been made by you; which is in all things and above all things, ruling and governing the universe with the greatest wisdom. Thus, by these things By these most sacred testimonies, therefore, most sacred Caesar Maximilian, I think it has been sufficiently proved that this whole universe is governed by the providence of God. Since he is pure understanding, simple, uncreated, and eternal, he knows all things, understands all things, and fully comprehends all things; and since he is omnipotent in nature, being able to do all things, he can do all things. Nothing is difficult for him, nothing impossible. He created such wondrous things by his power, established them in truth, perfected them by reason, sustains them by might, and illuminates them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory, who lives and reigns, God glorious and exalted, forever and ever. Amen.

THE AUTHOR'S PROTESTATION TO CAESAR.

These, most invincible Caesar Maximilian, are the things that seemed to me should be said in reply to the eight questions proposed by your majesty. For you wished to have my judgment also on the same matters in writing, making an estimate of me beyond the truth, of me, who am not to be compared in talent with those whose opinion you heard before mine. May pardon make me worthy if I have said anything less proper, since at the command of your highness, being a traveler set upon the road, I dictated as I could, at intervals, whatever occurred to me as needing answer.

I say, however, from my heart and openly protest that I am a sincere confessor of the Christian faith, and that I wish to remain until death in the union of the most holy Roman Church. Therefore, if anything either in this little work of mine or in others should be found said or written otherwise than that Church holds, thinks, believes, and teaches, I, as a true son of obedience, by the attestation of these presents declare and wish it simply to be, and to be held forever, revoked.

For this reason, most wise Caesar, I humbly beg and earnestly admonish your majesty that, before you cause my responses to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are being kept, you have them approved by the judgment of many. For the greatest care must be taken that nothing be proposed to those over whose salvation your serenity keeps watch unless it is solid, approved, manifest, and lawfully confirmed in the Catholic faith by the opinion of very many wise men. May almighty God direct and preserve you always by his providence, to the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors. From the city of Neometum, on the tenth day of the month of July, in the year of Christians one thousand five hundred and eight.

PRINTED AT FRANKFURT BY CYRIACUS JACOBUS.

In the year 1550.

PRINTED. IN THE HAND THE HEART OF THE KING OF THE LORD. 1220 Arist.
